speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week I gave the house first preliminary reports on the impact of Soviet nuclear tests as recorded by my department's network of air sampling stations. Final values have now been derived for the week ending September 10, and I would ask permission of the house to table a summary of these readings. I might mention that the highest level recorded in that period was 20 disintegrations per minute per cubic metre of air for Vancouver on September 9.
Yesterday afternoon we obtained first preliminary results on samples collected over last week end. These were from five of our air sampling stations in eastern Canada and show very sharp increases in fall-out levels. These results are as follows:

In commenting on these figures I might point out that the reading of 470 units for Toronto on September 16-17 is the highest ever recorded by my department since the beginning of our air sampling program in August, 1959. The fact that these readings have been observed within a very short time following the reported testing indicates that the measured activity is largely composed of short-lived fission products. This will be determined in subsequent analyses.
In my previous statement on fall-out levels I referred to the maximum permissible level derived from the recommendations of the international commission on radiological protection. I would again like to emphasize
90 units 260 units 100 units 215 units 75 units
140 units 90 units 80 units 470 units 200 units
that such figures are based on continued exposure at that level throughout a lifetime. Furthermore, the basic data provided refer to the long-lived component of a fission product mixture. As yet knowledge is incomplete concerning the significance of high levels of short-lived fission products. Such levels if maintained for a sufficient period of time might constitute a health hazard.
I would remind the house that the chief purpose of our air sampling program has always been to provide a method for the early detection of changes in the fall-out contamination of air all across Canada. We feel that more reliable information on the significance to health of fall-out can be obtained from other parts of my department's activities, such as the milk powder and bone sampling programs. In these programs we are concerned with the measurement of the specific components of fall-out which are likely to be of concern from the health viewpoint.
Such analyses are considerably more complex and are necessarily made on samples collected less frequently. It is too early yet to anticipate the levels which may be observed in this respect.

subtopic: FURTHER STATEMENT ON FALL-OUT RESULTING FROM RECENT TESTS
speechtext:
I think the house will agree that these reports of the Minister of National Health and Welfare are most important. It is desirable that he should make them and keep the Canadian people fully informed as to the readings of those various sampling stations which we now have in Canada.
It is clear that the increases are due to the recent Soviet union explosions. They cannot arise out of the tests made by the United States, because these latter explosions were in the laboratory and underground. It is therefore a matter of concern that the minister should report sharp increases in eastern stations. In one instance the testing showed the highest reading yet in the Canadian experience. The minister did not say whether these readings cover all the 13 explosions made by the Soviet union. Perhaps he will indicate at some time whether all the explosions of the Soviet union are covered by these recent tests.
The minister did not say so this morning in express terms, but in his statement last week he did say that while the explosions do show increased radioactive levels they do

Inquiries of the Ministry not indicate any appreciable increase in the danger to human health. That may be so, but I think more and more we are becoming concerned as a result of the division of opinion among scientists particularly as to the genetic danger to human beings. Some of them say that it will not be possible to determine the danger to human health for many years to come. This should put all nations on notice with respect to the undesirability of continuing these tests, particularly in the form in which they are now being carried out by the Soviet union.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
maintopic: CANADIAN POSITION RESPECTING APPOINTMENT OF SECRETARY GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman
was kind enough to inform my office in advance that he would ask this question. As he knows, the filling of the vacancy is provided for in article 97 of the United Nations charter, which reads in part as follows:
The secretariat shall comprise a secretary general .. . The secretary general shall be appointed by the general assembly upon the recommendation of the security council.
The procedure for filling the position either on an interim or permanent basis will be taken on the basis of that article. Talks are now going on among the delegations to find a solution. I think it would not be very helpful to go further than that at this time, except to say that the triple headed secretariat proposed by the Soviet union, which would be a self-cancelling body, is not acceptable to Canada. To set up such an organization in the form suggested by Mr. Gromyko yesterday


would mean that nothing of a controversial nature or unacceptable to the U.S.S.R. would ever be decided.
This matter raised by the hon. gentleman is one that all of us hope will permit of agreement, because until this matter is decided the future of the United Nations will always be uncertain. I know that people all over the world are hoping that a solution will be found that is reasonable, just, fair and equitable.

speechtext:
I should like to ask the Prime Minister a question arising out of reports of recent exchanges between Washington and Ottawa on the subject of the use by Canadian forces of nuclear weapons. Will the Prime Minister give the house an assurance that no

Inquiries of the Ministry decision will be taken regarding the acquisition or use of nuclear weapons by Canadian forces without parliament first having an opportunity to discuss such a decision?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: DISCUSSION BY PARLIAMENT OF USE BY CANADA
speechtext:
I noticed the news reports in question. I do not intend to refer to any personal correspondence because, as the Leader of the Opposition knows, there is continuing communication of a personal nature between heads of government; each corresponds with the other on a confidential basis, knowing that his confidence will be respected.
Discussions with the United States on defence subjects are going on at all times and at various levels. I reiterate what has been made clear on a number of occasions, except to those who will not understand. No agreement has been arrived at between our countries with regard to nuclear weapons, and any rumour to the contrary has no foundation in fact.
The government has undertaken to increase Canada's conventional forces to assist in meeting the more serious international situation which now confronts us. As was made clear during the discussion of the defence estimates we have also equipment which will enable the use of defensive nuclear weapons should the government decide that these are required in the interests of the national security. I might add that in February, 1959, and on subsequent occasions in the house I discussed the principles of our policy in that regard.
The government does not wish any decision that it may take in this matter to impede in any way any substantial progress which may be possible in disarmament or limitation on the spread of nuclear weapons to the independent control of countries not already having them.
I might also add that in the next couple of days important proposals may be put before the United Nations by the United States, following discussions with the United Kingdom, Canada and other nations, which we hope will bring about a new attitude in the field of disarmament. This is something in which this government has taken a commanding lead, and progress in this direction still remains our desire.
The announcement of decisions of government policy on this important issue will be made in the house. I might also say this; that the government, when placing such decisions before the house, will, naturally, at all times afford an opportunity for discussion. However, and I emphasize this, in each of the instruments that we have, the Bomarc and the Voodoos, nuclear weapons could be used. The defensive requirements of Canada


and the need for the preservation of security will be the overriding consideration in the mind of this government.
No decision has been made. When a decision is made the house will be clearly made aware thereof, as I emphasized a moment ago. Speculation which has been going on in the last few weeks is based on nothing more than the views of those who, desiring one final stand to be taken, are not taking into full regard the international situation nor in the event that it should worsen, the welfare, the future and the safety of Canadians.

speechtext:
the third reading of Bill No. C-71, respecting the civil service of Canada.

Civil Service Act

Mr. Speaker, the opposition will support this bill on third reading, for the reason that the Civil Service Act after 43 years was in need of revision, and no doubt in this bill there have been incorporated a number of changes that will bring the measure into conformity with modern practices that have developed in Canada in the intervening years. I wish to repeat what I said on second reading. This is not a new charter for the civil service, nor is it by any means a new deal for civil servants. This is the conception of the government and of the civil service commission.
One point that must be clearly stated at this stage before the bill passes is that the requests of the civil servants were not heeded in drafting this measure. Representatives of civil service associations appeared before the special committee and presented briefs and suggested amendments, but at no time were their suggestions accepted. Despite what has been said by the hon. member for Carleton, the hon. gentleman must realize that as far as the civil service associations are concerned they wasted their time in appearing before the special committee, because the government had a closed mind and the amendments advanced by the associations were rejected by the government majority on the committee.
These proposed amendments were repeated in the house by the hon. member for Hull, but were thrown out by the government one after the other. Those amendments represented the feelings of the employees of the government. They outlined the deal for which they were looking, and their requests fell on the deaf ears of this government.
The hon. member for Carleton on a few occasions admitted that the draftsmanship of this measure left something to be desired. I say with confidence that this measure will not survive for 43 years without amendment. Changes and amendments will have to be introduced from time to time because the faulty draftsmanship will come to light, and some portions of the measure will be found to be inoperative. There was no need to pass the bill in a hurry. An attempt should have been made to find better wording for use in some portions of the measure to satisfy the requests and requirements of the civil servants.
I repeat that this is not a new deal but merely a revision to bring the act into conformity with modern practice; that the requests of the civil service associations have been ignored, and that we on this side attempted on second reading to have the government consider the requests of employees of the civil service but met with no success.

Surely some government some day will recognize the rights of civil servants to deal with their employer as do other employees in industry.
Why did your government not do it over the 43 years?

That is a good question, but it is a very poor defence coming from a government which revised this act without taking into consideration the requests of the civil servants. The Liberal government embarked upon this revision of the Civil Service Act several years ago. The Heeney report was the result of an investigation ordered by Mr. St. Laurent. If the recommendations of the associations had been followed we would have the form of bargaining which I sought to advance in my amendment to section 7.
I repeat that this is not a new deal. This is a vast disappointment to civil servants and those who are close to them. Again I warn that the measure will have to be revised frequently. An employer cannot have working for him a group of dissatisfied employees. The government, above all others, needs the support of its employees. We on this side will support this bill in its present inadequate form, and look forward to the time in the near future when we will be given the opportunity to introduce the necessary amendments.

Mr. Speaker, it is always interesting to see how a transfer from the seats of government to those of opposition serves as a stimulus to thought. We regret that bargaining rights are not included in the bill presently before us. It is a well known fact that this is one of the things which we have campaigned for and advocated all across Canada for many years. I think it is also a fact that no Liberal government in any province, or in Canada, ever gave any consideration to this matter or ever established the right of bargaining for employees in the public service of the provinces or of the dominion.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Before the hon. member proceeds I should say that, although I did not interrupt the hon. member who preceded him, who was in pari delicto, as the lawyers say, I should remind him that the subject matter of the debate is the contents of the bill, not what is not in the bill. While I appreciate that the hon. member is not going to take any length of time, I think I should draw his attention to that point.

First I would say that it is regrettable to us that the bill contains the provision it does in clause 7 with respect to

consultation. In this regard it is a failure. I think it is regrettable also that the bill contains provision for infringement upon political rights and activities of employees in the public service. We dealt with this at the committee stage by way of amendment, and it is not necessary at this time to go over these particular matters again. But basically, so far as consultation and the relationships between the various associations in the civil service and the government itself are concerned, I think the provision is not such as to allow for any large degree of self determination on the part of the civil servants themselves with respect to their wages, hours of work and working conditions. It seems to me they will not be able to find proper, fair and adequate solutions to their particular problems by attempting to channel them through the restrictive conduit of the civil service commission, and that is what is necessary.
Apparently it is too late to do anything now because we are at this stage of the bill, and the government has not acceded to these legitimate and proper requests for one of the basic rights, namely to bargain collectively. Apparently sometime in the future we shall find that this provision will be contained in the act. I hope we do not have to wait for that long period of time until the Liberals get back into office, if they ever do, before we reach that particular stage.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the most astonishing statements that I have ever heard uttered in this House of Commons was that by the hon. member for Ottawa East, when he said that the voice of the civil service was not heard, and that at no time were the representations and the suggestions of the staff associations accepted. He suggested that for their part it was a waste of time to have come before the special committee.
Well, sir, I say that the facts controvert every statement made by the hon. gentleman. The fact is that the members of the staff associations have expressed themselves in the warmest possible terms on the treatment accorded to them by the special committee of this house. This special committee was one of the best committees it has ever been my privilege to sit on in this House of Commons. It was presided over by a very distinguished chairman of great ability, the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond (Mr. Mac-Lellan). Over a period of 26 or 27 sittings the committee gave the most detailed consideration to all the representations made.
What are the facts as to the attitude which the associations took after the hearings? I read from the letter of Miss Frances E. Goodspeed,
Civil Service Act
president of the professional institute of the public service of Canada. This letter is dated June 27, 1961, and is addressed to the chairman of the committee. It reads as follows: Dear Mr. MacLellan:
On behalf of my colleagues In the professional institute and myself may I express our appreciation of the opportunity which was afforded us to appear before your parliamentary committee on Bill C-71 and the careful consideration of our views on the subject matter of this bill by the committee.
Members of the professional institute who attended the sessions of your committee were greatly impressed with the very thorough and searching review which was given every section of the bill. We are confident that your efforts will result in a new civil service act which will afford an opportunity to continue in the future the development in Canada of a public service which will give the utmost satisfaction to the public in the discharge of its duties, personal satisfaction to those who seek therein a challenging and useful career, and which will gain even greater regard abroad than it currently enjoys.
How does that language stack up with the language we have just heard from the hon. gentleman from Ottawa East? In a statement issued by the head of a staff association representing 80,000 civil servants, Mr. White-house president of the civil service federation had this to say-

Mr. Speaker, it seems to me you admonished me for speaking about things which were not contained in the bill, and I acceded to your legitimate objection. I think perhaps the same rule should apply to the hon. member. He has not yet touched upon what is contained in the bill.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member is correct in principle, but of course before I appreciated that the debate was going beyond the scope of what is in the bill, or at least before I took any exception to it, a good deal had been said which is now in the course of being answered. It would not be fair to limit the answer, other than to remind the hon. member for Carleton, who is a very good parliamentarian, that what he is replying to perhaps should not have been permitted in the first instance, though that does not mean he cannot reply to it. If I have done any injustice to the hon. member for Skeena I am sorry, but that has been the result.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It appears that perhaps the hon. gentleman does not like this. I am sure the hon. member for Ottawa East would not like it. Mr. Whitehouse said this in his press release:
It is apparent that the government in providing for compulsory consultation has moved a long way towards giving public servants a voice in determining their rates of pay and conditions of employment. This is especially true in view of the statements made by the Minister of Finance

Civil Service Act
in committee that it was expected that the provisions for consultation would evolve into a system modified to meet the needs of the Canadian civil service.
The statement went on:
The civil service federation of Canada agrees to the foregoing with a view that experience will lead both sides to the evolution of a system of negotiation and arbitration in the shortest possible period of time.
At the same time the civil service association of Canada issued a statement. Unfortunately I do not have the full text of it in front of me at this moment, but I do have this, which I will quote:
There can be no doubt that the amended clauses represent improvement over the original forms of clauses 7 and 10.
The statement went on to express a preference for spelling out in the legislation the exact procedures on consultation and the results to flow therefrom. Then it ended in this way:
The civil service association of Canada will do everything possible to assist in working out proper machinery under the act. We will certainly do everything possible to contribute to an atmosphere of mutual trust and confidence in the period when such machinery is being developed.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker; does this type of language from all the major staff associations seem to indicate what the hon. gentleman from Ottawa East suggested, namely that the voice of the civil service was not heard? I say, sir, the voice of the civil service was heard. There was an opportunity over 26 or 27 meetings to consider in detail the amendments which were proposed by the staff associations, many of which were adopted by the special committee and last night were adopted in the committee of the whole.
I am sorry that in its final stages a partisan turn should have been given to the debate. I believe that in its day and age the 1918 Civil Service Act was a model of employer-employee relations. It established on a firm basis the merit system, a system which has given Canada a civil service of which every member of this house is proud. I believe that within the new 1961 Civil Service Act we have created a framework which will equally be a model in the future in the development of employer-employee relations. I believe it will stand as an example of the merit system which we in Canada will be able to say is not exceeded by any country in the world.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Chown in the chair.
DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR General administration-
178. Departmental administration including a grant of $10,000 to Frontier college and the expenses of the international labour conferences. $1,373,104.

Mr. Chairman, the minister made a statement in the two days that were taken up on these estimates before the adjournment. An examination of that statement, however, will reveal that the minister did little more than give us an account of the department's general activities. In no real sense did the minister address himself to what undoubtedly is the major domestic problem in Canada at this time; that is, the continuing problem of unemployment, a problem which in our opinion this government has not resolutely and forthrightly confronted.
Yesterday the departments concerned released the latest available figures, which were for the month of August, showing that as of that month 323,000 persons were unemployed. This represented a drop of some
31.000	from the corresponding period in the previous year. Nevertheless, not much satisfaction can be taken from this figure in spite of its improvement. It is also noteworthy that the labour force decreased by 39,000. It is significant that while unemployment dropped by 31,000 to 323,000 between July and August, unemployment nevertheless continues to be higher in Canada than in any other country of the western world. As long as there are these numbers of people out of work, with all that unemployment means, this government and all of us have a responsibility to try and correct this situation.
It is significant that while unemployment in August was below the total for the previous year, it represented 4.8 per cent of the labour force. That figure should give no one cause to gloat. The release, for instance-just to take a reference here and there-indicates that employment in Quebec decreased by
17.000	between July and August, which is somewhat more than usual even for this period. We see that in the Atlantic region employment declined by an estimated 12,000. Therefore when we compare these figures with countries that provide a basis for comparison, in this regard we continue to confront a problem that is of the greatest magnitude.
We must not forget that this is tradition ally not the slack period. We must not forget that in March of this year we had, on the

Supply-Labour
basis of the standard provided by the administration, 705,000 people out of work. It is important to note that the present standard of measurement does not take into account all those who are disengaged or who are out of work. It does not include people who work for less than 33 hours a week. Therefore I say that when we refer to our unemployment figures on the basis of these standards we should not think we have covered all those who are out of work.
When we think that Great Britain had to hire 500 Canadian men to assist in a supermarket project in that country, that is not something which should warrant our feeling that we are seriously coping with this problem. It should not give us any satisfaction to realize that on the basis of the report provided by the New York Times the rate of unemployment in Canada as of March was 11.1 per cent of the work force. In Australia, according to that survey, it was 3.4 per cent; in France, 3 per cent; in Germany, less than 1 per cent; in Great Britain, 1.6 per cent; in Israel, 7 per cent; in Italy, 5.4 per cent; in Japan, 1.1 per cent; in South Africa, 1.9 per cent; in Sweden, 1.7 per cent, and in the United States, 6.8 per cent.
In the face of all this I repeat that the government cannot, by its proper emphasis on other problems of a domestic and international character, seek to impress us that this is not a continuing, serious problem, because it is. Since this government came into power this country has experienced excessive unemployment, as we know. In 1958 some 7.1 per cent of our work force was out of work. In 1959 the figure was 6 per cent, and in 1960 it was 7 per cent. Moreover, we know that at one point this year almost 12 per cent of the work force of Canada was out of work. During the current year unemployment has never fallen below 6 per cent of the labour force after allowing for seasonal factors. These excessive levels of avoidable unemployment sap the vitality of our nation, deprive us forever of the wealth and products which could have been produced at full employment levels and, more important, have a devastating impact on the personal lives of the unemployed.
We have also at our disposal the various studies which were provided by the other place, studies which could have been provided by the House of Commons if we had had a willing administration which wanted to recognize that we had a responsibility in this elected chamber. Nevertheless, the excellent manpower study conducted by the Senate last year estimates that one million additional jobs will be needed by 1965 in order to accommodate the estimated growth in our labour force and get the rate of unemployment down to a reasonable proportion. Therefore it will

not be sufficient for the government to claim month after month that more Canadians are working than ever before.
A significant fact is that unless the government takes action, more Canadians than ever before will be unsuccessful in obtaining work. It is suggested that 3 per cent of our labour force is the maximum rate of unemployment that we can permit. Our objective, of course, should be to see to it that all Canadians are at work. That is the objective of the Liberal party in the program which has been stated in this house and which I propose, before I resume my seat, to repeat. That program, if implemented by this government, would provide a solution to this problem, as no other proposals put forward by this government or by any other political group are capable of doing.
In the Canadian economy long term unemployment, that is unemployment extending for more than 15 weeks during the year, is tending upward at a discouraging rate. My examination of the unemployment figures shows, for instance, that on the basis of the information presented yesterday, in August of this year 117,000 of the unemployed have been seeking work for over four months. This represents more than one third of the total number of unemployed in Canada, and
16,000	more than the unemployed in this particular category in August of 1960.
A long period of unsuccessful job seeking represents a real crisis in the personal life of an individual and an irrecoverable loss, both to himself and to the economy, of his productive capacity which goes unused during that time. The available statistics actually underestimate the amount of long term unemployment, for the labour force survey gives us only a snapshot at one point in time of those who have been continuously unemployed for a long period. However, a high proportion of those who have been out of work for 15 weeks of the year have more than one spell of unemployment per year, so they would not show up as having been unemployed for over three months on any given survey date.
We cannot blame the growth in the labour force, as the minister is apt to do, for this phenomenon, for the fastest growing components in the labour force are women and young men who do not suffer from unemployment. Growth in long term unemployment is due to basic changes in the structure of the economy, a decline in agriculture, in the extractive industries, railroads and so on. Workers in specific geographic areas have been victims of plant shutdowns or relocations. Many factors contribute to an excess of supply over demand for labour for long periods in distressed areas, factors such as the immobility of

labour, about which I shall have something more to say when I discuss the question of distressed areas.
What about this government's program for assisting distressed areas, by the way? What are the latest figures as to the number of areas that have been designated for assistance under this government's anaemic program deriving from the announcement made by the Minister of Finance last December of the government's plan to allow double depreciation; this program which has become, in the judgment of all responsible persons, a farce? It has, of course always been difficult to conceive how a program which provided for depreciation allowance in respect of one year only could be capable of meeting the serious problem which confronts us.
Even if we had full employment at the national level the minister recognizes, I am sure, that automation and the immobility of labour would leave us with pockets of high unemployment. Such is the character of our economy as it has taken on its present form, particularly during the past three or four years. The inability of the government to promote measures to ensure full employment at the national level has tended to aggravate the problem of regional unemployment. Many people living in areas of high unemployment lack a gainful livelihood for prolonged periods. The loss of income at the personal level results in the community being unable to provide even essential services.
Coupled with this deficiency, the problem of providing welfare for the unemployed in turn becomes impossible. The federal government is not seeking to overcome this problem. It comes forward with assistance to small business; it comes forward with a program of vocational training and so on, but all these things are of long term consequence. What the government fails to produce is a crash program, something which would provide immediate relief for the thousands who are still out of work. Failing such action, according to the advisory committee of the unemployment insurance commission, unemployment this coming winter will reach proportions similar to the figures of the past winter. Should this be the case the government has no excuse now, after the experience of three years, for failing to come forward with a crash program, as well as its long term program, to meet the situation.
To overcome this problem the federal government must aid in regional planning and supplement the financial capacity of the various regions to implement a region wide plan by means of federal grants and credits so the unemployed will have jobs to move to 90205-6-543J
Supply-Labour
and, what is more important, by means of tax incentives promote the location of industry in distressed areas.
I have a great deal to say on these estimates, and under our procedure it will not be possible for me to say all I have to say at this time. However, I propose to deal with a number of matters before these estimates are passed. I wish particularly to deal with the manner in which this government has escaped its responsibility in connection with the amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. I wish to deal with the contemptuous way it has treated parliament in deciding to establish a royal commission to assume the responsibility which, in the month of January, this government said it was going to assume by bringing forward a bill during the present session of parliament. But I shall say more on that subject later on.

The hon. member for Essex East has mentioned that the rules governing this committee will not permit him to carry on beyond a limited time. May I say it would be very acceptable to us if the hon. member were to be allowed unlimited time in this regard.
The minister is indeed very generous, and I thank him.

The minister is among those who take the position that all we do is criticize the government, and then the minister asks what we would do. That reply frequently is echoed in certain newspapers in our country. The suggestion is that all the Liberals do is criticize, that we never put forward a positive program.
The fact is that we have repeatedly in this chamber put forward our ideas as to how this problem can be met. I am going to repeat that program today so the country will know that not only have we indicted the government for its failure to deal with this problem, but at the same time we have a positive approach to the solution of the problem. Our solution is predicated on the belief that the freedom and integrity of our society depend on our being able to minimize the severity

Supply-Labour
of all that is involved in a high level of unemployment. Let us examine what we would propose to do.
1.	We would first of all transfer the responsibility for unemployment from the Department of Labour to the government as a whole. That in no way is a reflection on the minister himself. We maintain that the Department of Labour as presently constituted is not in a position adequately to deal with this problem.
2.	We would establish a national advisory council to deal with the problems of economic development, automation and employment.
3.	We would reassess federal agencies concerned with unemployment for the purpose of greatly extending their job finding function, of helping willing potential workers to find jobs outside of labour surplus areas, of intensifying vocational training programs. I shall have something to say about the vocational training program of the government later on. At first glance the program of the government may appear sound, but it is not providing results of the type which it was intended to provide, as I shall show particularly when I examine the situation in certain Canadian communities with regard to unskilled workers.
4.	We would integrate a flexible monetary policy with a fiscal policy suitable to the promotion of growth. In passing I should like to say that the government at long last has accepted the position we have taken with regard to its responsibility in the matter of monetary policy. The statement of the present governor of the Bank of Canada and that of the present Minister of Finance reflects what we have been contending all along. If this government had recognized earlier its responsibility in that regard, it is highly likely that the problem of unemployment would not be as severe as it has been and continues to be.
5.	We would balance the budget at full employment levels giving tax rebates during periods of recession and refunding the public debt during periods of expansion.
6.	We would introduce tax measures that would provide exemptions to encourage enterprise and increase private investment which, by the way, has drastically fallen since 1960. We would provide exemptions of a type that would encourage industry to locate in depressed areas. We would provide such policies as would encourage an improvement in our export position. We would provide a real accelerated depreciation program, one that would be a real encouragement to industry, not the kind of anaemic program presented by the Minister of Finance, jointly administered by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Labour; a program which I venture

to suggest will, by the revelation of the latest figures, prove to be absolutely ineffective in providing substantial employment in Canada.
I would be surprised today if the Minister of Labour could point to one instance of an individual being employed in Canada as a result of the double depreciation program.
We would provide encouragement, then, through an accelerated depreciation program, through depletion allowances, through special treatment of retained earnings that are actually invested, and through lower corporate taxes on increased export activities. These are the things which must be resorted to if we are going to stimulate our economy and provide the level of employment which our people expect and which this government in 1957 and 1958 assured the Canadian people it would effect.
7.	We would modify the present winter works program. We believe that the federal government should pay a higher percentage of the total cost and not just part of the labour costs on municipal projects. We believe that federal assistance should be given on a sliding scale measured in terms of the gravity of the local unemployment situation.
8.	As we indicated at our convention last January, we would establish a municipal loan fund to enable local governments to participate in intergovernment make-work schemes. This would have a special meaning for such areas as the Atlantic provinces. We would provide a shelf of public works to be implemented at the local level, federal assistance being conditional on implementation of projects during the periods of high unemployment. We recognize that while much can be done in this particular there are limitations that attend such a program.
Mr. Chairman, may I call it one o'clock?
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, to continue the program of the Liberal party, as a means of dealing with this major program, No. 10, we would provide for massive vocational and retraining programs to up-date the skills of the labour force, similar to what was accomplished during the war. Supplementary benefits paid to those willing to undergo instruction training should be provided.
No. 11, we would provide for increased public investment. Not merely would we divert investment from private sectors to the public sectors, but we would provide increased public investment itself.

Additional expenditures on central public services, hospitals and the like, provide an avenue of assistance that would help to stimulate the economy. This was noted by the mayors and municipalities of Canada at the recent meeting of the Canadian federation when it was observed that in every community across Canada there exists a great and growing backlog of essential community requirements of which the most urgent are housing, hospitals, schools, recreational facilities, renewal of blighted areas in the central core of our cities, civic centres, streets, highways, bridges and public transit to facilitate movement in our rapidly growing cities; underground service for water supply and food disposal.
In addition, we would provide assistance to secondary industry. Secondary manufacturing industries must play an increasingly important role in providing both uprising employment and income. Healthy expansion of these industries calls for special measures to increase both their markets at home and abroad. Tax measures should be used to encourage our domestic manufacturing industries to expand their exports, and incentives should take various forms such as reduction in the tax on the earnings of business, where there follows an increase of export sales. I made mention of this earlier but I have dealt with it a little more particularly now.
There must be stimulation of our export industry. The new Liberal government would take the initiative in actively pursuing, with other members of the organization of economic co-operation and development, all possible methods of freeing trade and expanding employment in the Atlantic area.
We ought to provide for more flexible forms of credit for industry and consumers. There is need for improvement in our financial machinery, in order to increase the availability of capital for the establishment, expansion and development of industries. We would see to it that adequate credit is available for the growth of industry. We recognize that there are special responsibilities of the federal government toward certain areas in Canada. I have mentioned distressed areas, but with special mention, I should like to note the assistance that we believe should be provided now for the Atlantic region. We believe that there should be measures to encourage the expansion of industry and employment in the Atlantic provinces. We have set forth in the resolutions of the January convention the details of this objective.
All the economic policies of a Liberal government, Mr. Chairman, would be directed toward recreating an environment in which Canadians can work, save and invest with confidence in the growth of the country and
Supply-Labour
its stability. It will be said, as it has been said, that when in opposition we take a bold and forthright position. The fact is that when we were in office, notwithstanding what hon. gentlemen may say, we did provide the highest level of employment that this country has ever enjoyed. At no time during the period when we were able to resuscitate ourselves from the consequences of the 1930-35 depression did unemployment ever reach anything over 3 per cent of the total work force. Hon. gentlemen may trot out figures for this particular year or that particular month, but the record is there for everyone to examine. No one will be able to contend that there was any period, during the time when we were in office, that is comparable with the situation now confronting us. But even if there was, that does not absolve this government from its responsibility in the face of this serious problem.
This problem is one that must be resolved if we are going to preserve, as I said a moment ago, the integrity and character of our free society. There are many things that the government can do now. Over four and a half months ago we had presented to us the Bladen commission report, a commission appointed by the government to examine into the state of the automobile industry, but we have not had any indication from the government whatsoever of its intention to implement that report. It is true that the assistance that was given by a reduction in the excise tax was a recommendation of the commission. This reduction had been urged in the house, and hon. gentlemen who refer to that as an acceptance of the Bladen report will find themselves not fully demonstrating that they have exhausted their reading of that report. Why should there be this delay in examining and accepting either in whole or in part the proposals made by that royal commission with regard to a very vital industry in our country or providing alternatives to those proposals?
True, the government brought forward legislation last fall to provide for vocational training. We were told, as I have reminded the house on a number of occasions, that the chairman of the unemployment insurance commission said that only one in ten of the unemployed in our country possesses a skill that would enable him to assume a particular job there available. That is a serious situation. True, the government brought forward an amendment to the vocational training act. We pointed out at that time that those provisions were not generous enough to meet the problem, and I have before me pretty strong supporting evidence of the grounds that we took at that time.

Supply-Labour
I understand, for instance, that in the city of Toronto alone there was recently produced a figure of 2,642 unemployed Toronto men and women who were barred from participating in the retraining program set up for them. That figure represents 70 per cent of the applicants for retraining. I say that a scheme which overlooks 70 per cent of the applicants is obviously inadequate. One might well say, what kind of a program is it that turns down three quarters of the jobless people it is intended to help?
The real reason for this, of course, is that the vocational training courses being offered under the combined federal-provincial assistance program require grade 10 qualifications and most of the applicants in this figure of 2,642 do not possess a grade 10 certificate. There is an obvious remedy for this situation and that is to offer academic subjects in the program. We want to provide education to men and women so that they can be fit to take on jobs that are available to them. We should now recognize that the vocational training act must be amended to provide this recognition of the need of training persons with education below grade 10 level, so that they can have the necessary academic background to take added training and in turn to provide them with the kinds of skills essential at this time.
These are just two of the things I mention to indicate that the government is really not meeting this problem head on. The government as a whole has not engaged in a process of planned effort. I do not mean planned effort in the sense in which that term is used by those who would build up a state octopus. I do not believe in the planning to which some totalitarian countries of communist or other types have resorted to, but the kind of planning necessary at this time, if we are going to have a successful confrontation of this problem. These two isolated cases demonstrate how the government has not engaged in a process of planned programming to try to meet the problem. That is why we find ourselves face to face almost every day with evidence which shows the lack of a dynamic and complete approach by the government to this whole problem.
On these estimates there is one other matter which I have foreshadowed and about which I would like to say something. We were told by the Minister of Labour on May 9 last that a carefully thought out program of amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act would be brought before parliament this session. We were told that the government had made a study of the report of the advisory committee of the unemployment insurance

commission and that as a result of the government's study of that report it had come to the conclusion that the problem facing the authorities could not be met simply by appropriating money to meet the payments which would be required to bolster the fund. The important thing is that the minister told us that the program would be brought down in parliament during the course of the session in which we were then, as now, engaged.
This intention was referred to, of course, by the government in the speech from the throne, in the month of January, when the government announced that legislation would be brought forward at this session to provide amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act to deal with substantive features of the act as well as to provide for the kind of economic cushioning, necessary because of the perilous financial state into which the fund had been plunged. We were told, as I say, about the government's intention in the month of January. It was confirmed during a speech made by the Minister of Labour in this house on May 9 and confirmation of the government's intention was repeatedly given by responses to questions put by members of the Liberal opposition during the course of the present session of parliament. About two days before we adjourned in July I asked the government when it was going to bring down these amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. The Minister of Labour told us that that matter was still under study. The implication was clear, that when we resumed we would have before us the amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act and that we, in this house, would give consideration to those amendments.
A little more than a week after we adjourned in July an announcement was made in the press, I think it was on July 25, that the government had appointed a royal commission. The Prime Minister did not use the words "royal commission", but he said they had appointed a committee. This committee was to go into the whole question of the proposed amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. The Prime Minister mentioned in his statement the financial state of the fund, thereby indicating that this committee would also examine into that problem. I say, Mr. Chairman, this is not the first time this government has resorted to this particular device, leading the house to believe in the dying days of the session that it was going to carry forward with its program announced in the speech from the throne and then the moment we were out of this chamber, no longer face to face with the Minister of Labour, the government announces a device by which it hopes to remove from this

house not only the responsibility for formulating a policy but for discussing the measure prior to the formulation of that policy. This act was an act that can only be branded as one that holds parliament in contempt.
This was not the first time this had been done. We will all remember that just before parliament adjourned in the summer of 1960, I asked the Minister of Labour to table the latest report of the advisory committee of the unemployment insurance commission. He said it was not available and within a few hours of our adjourning, in a manner that defied our examining the report, the report was placed on the table through the Clerk. We had prorogued, as a matter of fact, before we learned the contents of that report. Parliament was denied, then, the opportunity of discussing the terms of that report, just as we are now being denied the opportunity of knowing what the government's policy is with regard to amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act.
The government said it had a policy in January. It told us the same thing on May 9 and yet, within a few days of our leaving this house it announced that instead of the policy being formulated by the government, it was going to appoint a royal commission to examine into the whole state of the unemployment insurance fund, to provide suggestions for amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. I say, Mr. Chairman, that act on the part of the government is one that shows the government's contemptuous regard for this parliament. We should in this session be dealing with the unemployment insurance amendments. We should not leave this subject to gentlemen outside of this house. This is our responsibility. The government said it was our responsibility in January. What has intervened in the meantime to cause the government to change its position?
Is it because the government has not the courage to face the issues that will be projected as a result of gaps that exist in the Unemployment Insurance Act? This is not the first time, as I say, that the government has resorted to this device. I regret that the Minister of Labour should be the tool of the government in this devious practice of not recognizing the pre-emptive right of parliament in these matters. Of course, this device of this government, the appointment of royal commissions, is not new. In the course of three and a half years this government has appointed 14 royal commissions to assume responsibilities which the present Prime Minister said, when he was in opposition, were those which should be borne by the government as a whole. These are devices which fool no one. These are devices to enable the government to escape its responsibilities, to
Supply-Labour
enable it to say to the Canadian people, "Oh well, we could not bring forward a definite policy with regard to this matter for the simple reason that matter is now being studied by a royal commission."
You know, a royal commission is sacrosanct. It is difficult to discuss a subject that is before a royal commission. It is argued here that this government, by the use of this device of appointing royal commissions, has not removed from us in this house the responsibility of examining these matters. We have before us the latest report of the advisory committee of the unemployment insurance fund. I would be interested in knowing how many members have read this report. Those who have read it will come to the conclusion, that it is most regrettable we are denied the opportunity of examining the unemployment insurance amendments and considering the government's policy for replenishing the fund. The fund has reached a perilous state. The unemployment insurance fund will be down to its last penny by early 1962, so the committee points out, unless the government replenishes the fund in some way. The committee points out that with another winter of high unemployment the fund may be expected to be empty entirely by next May. It points out that the balance in the fund has been skidding for three years. It was $184,685,000 on March 31, about half what it was the year previous, and this in the face of the fact the fund in 1956 stood at $962,726,930. The latest published figure, since the fund year ended on March 31, shows that at the end of July the balance was $120,771,909. The committee goes on to advise the government that it should make special grants to the fund from which unemployment insurance benefits might be paid in order to carry the fund over until the precarious state of the fund can be corrected by amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act.
Is it because of this report that this government has taken steps to deny us the opportunity of examining into something about which this government said in January, 1961, it had a definite policy. When we think, Mr. Chairman, that during the whole 20 years of this fund $3.25 billion have been paid out in unemployment insurance benefits, when we realize that in 1942 only $37 million was paid in benefits and that by 1958 the benefit total had reached $492.9 million, we see perhaps some of the provocation for the devious course the government is following in this matter through the appointment of a royal commission and its reluctance to do something which this government said in January last it was prepared to deal with in this house. These are matters the minister will have to explain. These are matters which he cannot leave untouched. He cannot say the government, in its

Supply-Labour
wisdom, has appointed a royal commission now and that it would not serve the national interest for us to take a course with regard to this matter that would in any way work against the careful and objective assessment of the royal commission. The royal commission has not yet begun its sittings. I venture to suggest that a federal election will be over before we get a report from the commission. We will not know for many months, for many months, for over a year, what amendments are going to be provided for with regard to the Unemployment Insurance Act and what this government is going to do to replenish the fund.
This is not a fund that belongs to parliament; this is not a fund that belongs to the government of Canada; this is a fund in the main which belongs to two segments of the Canadian population, the workers and the employers of Canada. It is their money. This government has used this money, and it owes it to those who are the beneficiaries of the fund, who are its owners, to explain what the government is going to do by way of bolstering that fund.
We would like to know, for instance, if it is the government's intention to bolster the fund by increasing contributions, without in any way providing an increase in the pattern of benefits, as was done two years ago That was a scandalous performance, increasing the contributions of the workers of this country at a time of high employment, without increasing the pattern of benefits.
These, Mr. Chairman, are some of the matters that engage our consideration as we begin once again to discuss the estimates of the Department of Labour. I hope before the Minister of Labour allows these estimates to pass he will indicate that the government is not sitting back complacently with regard to this problem of unemployment; that it is not drawing the conclusion that because the figure for the last reported period shows a drop of 31,000 in the number of unemployed, everything is well. Let the minister take the committee into his confidence.
What are the prognostications of his department? There was a time-and I would be surprised if that practice did not still exist -when the Minister of Labour was furnished with quarterly assessments for the ensuing period. We have seen assessments as to what levels of unemployment are likely to persist during the fall of 1961 and the winter of 1962. The advisory committee of the unemployment insurance fund, a non-political body serving the government in an advisory capacity, tells us that unemployment in this period will be comparable to last year. If that is the case, what is the government going to do about it? Is it going to continue

in the way in which it has dealt with this problem over the course of the past three years, or is it going to come forward with a program, not only in the long term but to meet the existing social waste that flows from unemployment?
That is the main domestic responsibility of this government and no other issue, no matter how important it may be, on the domestic front or internationally can becloud the existence of this issue. This government cannot shrink from its responsibility. Let the government no longer say that it has not had suggestions from the opposition. Those suggestions were in large measure repeated by me today for the simple reason that I did not want hon. gentlemen opposite to say we had no suggestions to make, repeating the suggestion they have made from time to time to the effect that we do not have a positive program.
We were not elected to deal with this problem. The responsibility is one that primarily rests on the government. If it has no program, then let it adopt the Liberal party program. If it does that, we will find that Canada will gradually be restored to the high economic state it had when in 1957 we left office. That is the challenge I put forward.
The Minister of Labour has an opportunity to examine every one of these proposals. Let him tell the committee whether the government subscribes to them or not. If he does not accept those proposals, what does he offer? To tell us that the government is going to continue with its double depreciation program will certainly be a farcical answer because that program can only be described as one capable of producing little, if anything at all.
The government's winter works program, good in principle, obviously does not go far enough. Amendments are proposed by us and by the organization of mayors and municipalities. This is not a federal program. The minister talks about this winter works program as though it were the responsibility of the federal government. It is the program of the municipalities of Canada and the provinces of Canada; they pay two thirds of the cost of the program. Yet this government parades across the country, referring to its achievement in terms of solving unemployment by its winter works program, a program that basically, in a titular way, belongs to the provinces and municipalities and to which the federal government is only one third a contributing party and to which it does not contribute as much as the other two parties.
Let this government realize that it has thus far failed to meet its responsibilities

in this field. Let it courageously tell the house and the country what it proposes to do to bring about a mitigation of this, the most serious domestic problem in our country.

Mr. Chairman, it is always interesting to listen to the hon. member for Essex East. However, I often wonder why his actions when in office did not meet his eloquence and the embracing of particular ideas that he now espouses.
Of course, they did.

The hon. member says they did. Of course, the record will show the position to be completely otherwise. It is not my intention to again enter into an extensive discussion of matters coming under the jurisdiction of the Department of Labour, for this was done earlier this session when the estimates were considered before the recess.
However, there is one matter of general importance and general concern that took place after parliament recessed in the summer and about which the hon. member for Essex East spoke at some length. I should like to make a comment or two in this regard. I refer to the appointment of the royal commission to deal with the Unemployment Insurance Act.
All this indicates to me is that the government itself, and perhaps even the minister, is void of opinions and policies on what should be done with respect to unemployment insurance and has used the means of the appointment of some study group to deal with the matter in the hope that it can prevent itself being criticized for delay and procrastination on this very, very important matter.
It would not surprise me in the least, with the expectation that we may have a federal election next year, if this royal commission report were just coincidentally made available at the time of that election so the Prime Minister could tour the country waving this royal commission report, along with all the other royal commission reports, in front of the general public saying to them, as the Prime Minister is so able to say, "All you have to do is just re-elect me and these things will come into effect tomorrow". We all know, of course, that the past record of this government and of the Prime Minister particularly shows that actions while in office have no connection whatsoever with lavish promises made before an election. I wish the study group well in its considerations and in its discussion of the Unemployment Insurance Act and of the fund itself. Certainly there are hundreds of thousands of people in this
Supply-Labour
country who are concerned about these subjects and who have been concerned about them for years. So, naturally, the government should be concerned about this field. As I say, I wish this study group well and I hope it comes up with some sensible and fair recommendations for changes which will be found acceptable by the government in office. However, the experience of past practice leads me to believe that the government will not give too much consideration to what this commission or study group recommends. A few years ago an investigation was made into another matter of concern to the people of Canada, and the result of that recommendation is referred to now as the Clark report. This was an urgent matter in 1957 and 1958-[DOT] urgent only because the Prime Minister wanted to use it as an election gimmick. That report has been filed with the government for a long time, now, but so far all we have discovered is that the Minister of National Health and Welfare has lost it or, as the phrase goes, is giving it consideration. I doubt very much whether the Prime Minister or the government intend to take any action with regard to it.
There was a report made to the government by the royal commission on publications but so far nothing has been heard of it. I suppose that has got lost, too. The report of the royal commission set up to inquire into the automobile industry, known as the Bladen commission, is another report which has been by-passed and pushed into some dusty closet. In this connection I recall reading some Conservative party propaganda published back in 1957 in which the present Minister of Labour was lauded as being the sole and only expert in Canada on the automobile industry. In any event, we had a royal commission to investigate that matter and the report has been lost. There was a report and recommendations with respect to national fish marketing questions but so far the minister and his colleagues have pushed them to one side. Thus, as I say, past experience indicates that this so-called royal commission appointed to deal with the Unemployment Insurance Act, the commission and the fund is nothing more than a subterfuge to enable the government to get out from under a difficult problem about which it intends to make no decision anyway. In this regard the government operates in an ostrich-like fashion, as does the Minister of Finance in particular, hoping that things will get better in the coming year and giving that as an excuse for doing nothing. I think that is a disgraceful manner in which to treat working class people-to shift these all-important matters on to a royal commission or study

Supply-Labour
group and then, when money has been spent on making the report, to file that report away and forget about it.
One specific matter I should like to deal with relates to wages, hours and working conditions in the H.M.C. Dockyard in Halifax and particularly those of tradesmen employed in the yard. As far back, at least, as 1950 -and this includes the period when the hon. member for Essex East was in office-there has been dissension between the employees working in that yard and the government because of the attitude taken by the government with regard to wages, especially the wages paid to tradesmen. There is a system in effect-what the formula is it is impossible to discover-which allows the government to conduct surveys from time to time in private industry in the particular area around Halifax and by some magic formula determine what the prevailing or average rate of pay is. This average is then applied to the workmen in the dockyard. This is what causes the disagreement, the hard feelings and the bitterness, in many instances, of the employees working there toward this government and other governments which have held office.
In the past the government has been inundated with letters, telegrams, personal visits, telephone calls, briefs, presentations, arguments and the like from employees and unions representing those employees in the dockyards about this question of prevailing rates and the rate applicable in the yard itself. So far, no answer has been given. So far over all the years all the employees have got is the run-around, being pushed from one department to another. The question has been referred to interdepartmental committees for study and report but no action has been taken toward a solution, nor is there any indication that a solution will be arrived at. As a result the government cannot expect anything else but disagreement and hard feelings to develop, together with occasional walkouts on the job. As I say, this has been going on for at least ten years and the position has become even more difficult in the last few months. At one time there used to be an arrangement with regard to certain tradesmen under which rates were known as starred rates, or what we might call red circle rates, under which an extra five cents an hour was paid. This was in recognition of efficiency and extra skill on the part of the individuals concerned. In May, 1960, there was a general five cent an hour increase in the rates of the industry itself. When this five cent increase was applied in the yard it was decided that the men getting the starred rates, or red circle rates, would not receive the five cent increase. In fact, they

lost five cents because of the attitude of the government. From that time on there were more briefs, more letters and more telephone calls to a variety of members of the cabinet but, once again, all the workers got was the run-around.
As a matter of fact, this question was dealt with by treasury board. The board discussed what was to be the position with respect to establishing a proper formula to govern the pay of the employees. Some time in April- I believe it was on April 17-the board decided that no change should be made in the formula, the reasoning being that it would not be economically sound to take a wage structure which applied to one section of the economy and superimpose the average on another section of the economy. This meant, for argument sake, that the treasury board said that the administration was not going to survey, say, the construction field and then decide that the prevailing rate, or the average rate, should be applicable to the dockyard workers. This would amount to taking results from one section of the economy and impinging them on another section, and for this reason the board decided that the old system should continue to prevail.
What position has been taken by the government with respect to other types of employees in the dockyard? With respect to carpenters and others it takes the prevailing rate applicable in the industry and applies it in the shipyard.
Surveys into the matter have been conducted by the unions in an attempt to find logical and statistical arguments to present to the government. As of July 5 of this year the prevailing rate for comparable work in Nova Scotia ran as high as $2.80 an hour but the rate applicable at the dockyard was $2.05 an hour. By virtue of the government's inherent laziness in dealing with difficult problems a discrepancy of that magnitude is permitted to exist. I submit this is not a sensible way for the government to behave, especially a government which espouses the ideas which the Prime Minister says it espouses. When treasury board met on this question it brushed aside the legitimate request of the men in the dockyard. I do not know why that was done unless, as I said, it was because the government is lazy in coming to grips with difficult problems.
There are several rankling features of the situation in the dockyard. Over the years these employees have attempted to have instituted a system of collective bargaining. They wish to sit down with their employer and discuss the question of a formula for applying prevailing rates. Even that small request has been denied them. No opportunity

has been given them to discuss this matter with those who make these decisions and impose them on the employees, usually without consideration as to the result. These people desire a fair formula and the right to enjoy collective bargaining. They merely wish the rights that are available to almost all other employees in the nation.
There is also concern about the question of check-off. I do not have details of the matter but I know the government will check off union dues for members of staff organizations and associations but does not have the decency to extend the same courtesy to those who are members of trade unions. I am sure this is not in keeping with the public utterances of the minister concerning the rights of employees in Canada. Possibly the minister is not aware of the situation. Perhaps it was not discussed at meetings he attended or perhaps he simply did not pay attention. In any event I put this matter forward now in a public way.
I am informed that on June 27 meetings were held at which these matters were discussed, the questions of a formula, check-off and collective bargaining. In the month of April the minister must have had some knowledge of this matter because he wrote a letter to the dockyard council saying that an interdepartmental committee had been set up as a result of these questions having been discussed. These committees offer little hope to the people on the job. They are not concerned with committees that meet in secret and which take no action. They are concerned with their basic right to enjoy some control over their own welfare, the right to discuss points of difference with their employer. The government should have the courtesy to advise the unions involved that an opportunity will be provided to discuss these points of difference in an attempt to reach a mutually agreeable solution.
I wish to point out to the minister that this problem will not be solved by interdepartmental committees. These have been established on this question before. The question was brushed aside by the committees and no conclusion was reached. Treasury board made the spurious decision to which I referred earlier. As a result of not adopting a fair formula some employees receive up to 75 cents an hour less than comparable employees elsewhere in the province engaged in private industry.
Because of the failure of the government to extend the courtesy to which I referred with respect to the check-off of union dues those outside the staff associations must wander about attempting to collect cash dues from
Supply-Labour
their members. The minister can appreciate how this interferes with the work force and contributes to a negative attitude.
In conclusion I say to the minister that the problem will not be solved by interdepartmental committees nor by letters to the effect that the matter is being given consideration, no matter what adjective is used to qualify the consideration. The minister must say to the council and the union that the government is prepared to sit down with them and negotiate these differences of opinion in an effort to reach a conclusion satisfactory to all. If the minister were to do that he would have taken a forward step toward reaching settlement of the difficulty and would remove any doubt that would tend to be cast on the sincerity of his public utterances.

Mr. Chairman, I was most impressed by the eloquent speech made in this chamber by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin). He is always interesting, and the only criticism I would address to him would be that he repeats a little too often previous statements made by him many times at the beginning of this session. I cannot blame him because, as I just said it is always a pleasure both for government and opposition members to listen to the hon. gentleman.
Mr. Chairman, I have no intention today of dealing with a controversial issue; neither do I have any desire to discuss the particular arguments brought forth in the course of this debate by the hon. members of the opposition. I would rather deal with a general issue of great interest to me and which in my opinion should also be of interest to all the right-minded Canadians. I am referring to the economic freedom in Canada.
Freedom, our most precious right in this world, as it was so well described by the great French writer, Louis Veuillot, inspires good thinking and I noticed when I was preparing my remarks that thoughts along that line are not always easy to express. I therefore ask the house to be indulgent for someone treading on ground as difficult as world economy.
The person who can act without restraint, while abiding by the laws, enjoys civil liberty, from which stem liberty of thought and action on temporal and spiritual things.
Canada certainly has just as much wealth of civilization if not more than her neighbours.
The faculty we enjoy of acting, speaking and writing freely is however submitted to

Supply-Labour
the free right of criticism which is rarely unemployed here in Canada. Criticism can be severe at times, and Sir Wilfrid Laurier used to say that it uses a sprinkler which often has the appearance of a bludgeon.
Criticism might be severe and refuse to admit certain views I express, but I do not think it can lessen my sincerity. It is a well known fact that the majority of the Canadian population is of French or English descent and that it has a leading influence. However, that influence does not allow us to ignore that Canadian freedom, during the last 60 years, has been generously granted to an important part of our population which is of other descents.
Thousands of immigrants, indeed millions, have come from almost all the European countries. Many of them settled in our cities, but the majority chose our western prairies. They took advantage of our naturalization act, thus securing the franchise and the consequential freedom to discuss with us our national issues.
In the economic structure of Canada, their intellectual influence and their material wealth cannot be ignored.
For Canadians whose forefathers settled in this country long ago, whether French or English speaking, as well as for Canadians by adoption, the freedoms of thought, of speech, of writing, and the right to pray, to own properties and to vote are the same. The privilege of being a free man in a biethnical and bicultural country is one of the greatest advantages that is fortunately to be found in our country.
In the province of Quebec, we enjoy this great privilege of having for our mother tongue the French language which has the fluidity of running water and the resistance of metal, as a great French writer so well described it.
Moreover, we enjoy this freedom of religion which has enabled us to build churches in our cities where we may pray God in the caith of our parents or that of our choice.
In addition to this freedom of speech, of religion, of action and of opinion, we enjoy economic freedom that permits us to convert into riches the products of the soil with which Providence has so generously endowed all parts of our country. The material results obtained are impressive:	transcontinental
railways whose facilities are being constantly improved, civil and commercial aviation, the building of the St. Lawrence seaway, huge Canadian factories, agricultural products of which wheat alone represents up to 500 million bushels-
