Mr. Chairman, I feel constrained to rise on a point of order. My point of order is that we are considering the estimates of the Department of Labour, the conduct of the Minister of Labour, and presumably those problems directly associated with his department. I am just wondering whether the Associate Minister of National Defence has not made a mistake about the audience to which he is speaking and perhaps the speech he intended for the Richelieu club is being delivered here instead.

Mr. Chairman, on the point of order, may I say first of all that when I started my remarks I said that I was going to speak on a general theme. I am trying to give a general description of the advantages which we have in Canada which to my way of thinking permit us to say that the economic situation, far from being as bad as hon. members of the opposition would like the Canadian people to believe is on the contrary a very strong, very potent and very rich one, and that we have every reason to be proud of the results which have been achieved. The fact that, in spite of the prophecies of gloom which we have heard so frequently from hon. members opposite, this government has succeeded in defeating the economic recession which was threatening the nation, is to its credit and its honour.
At long last we are on the way to our new and ever higher destinies. This has been done by various methods which I should like to explain to the committee, and which I am sure are just as interesting to the committee as the eternal prophecies of gloom and doom which we have heard so frequently from hon. members opposite.
If the hon. member will permit me to continue my remarks I shall do so, and I would appreciate it if he did not interrupt me any more than we did when he repeated the same old speeches which we have heard so frequently in the house.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Perhaps I should intercede just briefly to indicate that I was listening carefully to the minister. I am inclined to the view that a general discourse on the economy of the country as a whole or of the entire world would be straying a

little far from the narrower subject that is before the committee for consideration.
I have made it a practice, as hon. gentlemen know, to allow a pretty wide scope of debate on item No. 1.
I hope that no member or minister will take advantage of this generous spirit by wandering too far from the topic under consideration.

I will certainly abide by your ruling, Mr. Chairman. I was trying to point out in the earlier part of my remarks that in Canada we have a tremendous development program which, if you look at the potential of the nation, is really only in its initial stages. My remarks were intended to indicate that, far from being pessimistic concerning the difficulties which we have experienced in the past and which we may experience again, we have in the contrary every reason to be optimistic because though we have had problems during the last two years we seem to have found the proper solutions and today we are marching toward ever greater prosperity and certainly toward progress.
(Translation):
Mr. Chairman, I should like to revert to the use of the French language to continue the remarks I was making when I was interrupted by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill).
And rightly so.

As I was saying, I listened to the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) who, explained to us once more before recess, what he said many times in this house when he gave figures on the unemployment situation in Canada, during the past few years. As a matter of fact, we were worried about the unemployment which was prevailing in Canada and which seemed to threaten our economy and the present and future welfare of our fellow citizens.
It is precisely because we were worried about the consequences of unemployment that the government introduced measures which made it possible to cope with the existing difficulties.
For instance, with a view to activating the circulation of money, which means greater buying power for individuals, we have asked the chartered banks to guarantee loans to small industries that need money to build or improve their plants.
Because we have recognized the fact that most of the unemployed are labourers, this
Supply-Labour
government has contributed to a large extent to the establishment of schools which the unemployed of this country can attend to learn a trade, because the government realizes that construction is an essential factor in our country's prosperity.
Billions of dollars have been loaned to Canadian builders and to the citizens who want to build their own homes. This was done through the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
Precisely because this government knows it is essential to have close co-operation between capital, labour and government, we have decided to call together in a productivity council the heads of the major Canadian industries, the heads of the main labour unions in the country, the people who are experts in economics, industry and all other fields. It is by uniting those three forces-labour, capital and government-that we succeeded in finding formulas that made it possible for our economy to spring back to new life and soar to new heights.
Mr. Chairman, we are happy to find that all our efforts have been successful, since unemployment is not only decreasing but everything shows that the proportion of Canadian workers who are unemployed will continue to decrease. The forecasts for coming years are excellent and even give a promise of unprecedented prosperity.
For instance, allow me to point out that this reduction in unemployment is felt in the district I represent here in this house, where there are about 171,000 workers. There were, last March, more than 6,500 unemployed in that district. Now, last Friday, I met the director of the unemployment insurance office who told me that this number had gone down, in the relatively short period of six months, from 6,500 to about 1,800, and he added that there was work for at least another 1,200 persons.
This is on account of Mr. Lesage's administration.

Just in order to show you that the reduction in the unemployment rate in the Longueuil area is very real may I point out that in the Nouveau Journal of Saturday last, we find full pages of ads put in by our merchants, industrialists or businessmen, offering jobs to potential workers.
This goes to show, Mr. Chairman, that the prophecies of doom and gloom we have heard repeatedly from hon. members opposite these last few months, were not based on facts but

Supply-Labour
rather on the only hope these gentlemen have, of regaining, at any price, the power which they lost in 1957, through their inertia, their incompetence and their long disinterest of public affairs.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to recall all the evil done to the renown of our country and, at the same time, to the welfare of our fellow citizens, by their constant harping on the fact that there is in Canada a certain degree of unemployment, as well as the exaggeration, constantly entertained by hon. members opposite, of the seriousness of this problem. I will not go as far as saying that the problem was not serious. I will not try to minimize the importance of taking care of those who are without work and of finding them a job so that they can play an important part in the economy of our country. On the contrary, we have been concerned with those who are without work. We have understood the hardships suffered in homes where the scourge of unemployment unfortunately strikes. As I just said, we have taken all the steps that we could take to check this scourge, and we already consider ourselves very fortunate for having succeeded in this.
I believe that it is in poor taste and surely not proper to constantly seek to blacken Canada's good name by over-emphasizing the seriousness of our economical situation. Last winter, in French and English newspapers, well-known journalists were writing articles telling the British, French, and other Europeans to forget Canada, to forget about coming to settle here and even to forget about investing money in our country because, as they said: "It is becoming more and more obvious, when reading Canadian newspapers and the criticisms made there, that Canada is a country suffering distress and hardship; Canada is no longer the land of tomorrow that we had heard of."
This reputation, given to Canada, is harmful and even disastrous. Moreover, it is not based on fact because Canada, far from being a land of hardship, as hon. members opposite have unfortunately too often tried to give the impression-only, as I say, in order to attain certain political ends-far from being a land of hardship, Canada, on the contrary, might well be the wealthiest country in the world. It is certainly the country where the future is most promising for those who want to start a family, establish a business or an industry, and prosper along with the country.
[Mr. Sevigny.l
Mr. Chairman, one only has to travel in foreign countries, to go to South America for instance, or Africa, or to look at what is happening in Asia, to realize that Canadians born here in Canada, or those who had the privilege of coming here to settle, are actually privileged, and that in fact it is in this country that we find true happiness and the best opportunities for prosperity and a happy future.
Mr. Chairman, I recently went to South America and I was able to witness the poverty of those who live in countries under an autocratic regime, or those whose countries are too often torn by internal revolutions. I saw there, Mr. Chairman, the havoc that communism can visit on a country when it permeates the social, cultural, intellectual and economic life of the nation.
I saw a country, such as Brazil, where out of a population of 70 million inhabitants, 35 million are illiterate and live in the most awful poverty. I saw that land which was called, not so long ago, "Brazil, land of the future", a country one step from bankruptcy, one step from ruin and one step from the most complete social upheaval.
In Argentina, which bears a striking resemblance to our country, from a cultural, social and economic point of view, I saw the threat of complete bankruptcy, and had it not been for the constructive genius of the man who is now that country's president, I think it would be today in the throes of revolution.
Why are those nations in such a state of distress, whereas we here in Canada today are enjoying prosperity, peace and what might be called almost full employment? This, Mr. Chairman, is due to the fact that over there, countries did not realize the greatness of that democratic freedom I mentioned at the beginning of my remarks. They failed to realize that it was by living in accordance with the democratic ideal and the philosophy of life which is ours, that a country could develop, prosper and aspire to still greater destinies. At the turn of the century, when they were offered the same chance as we were, they preferred to that democratic system, which gave us our strength which enabled us to develop and prosper and reach our present standards of living, an autocratic and despotic rule which destroyed all liberty. If I mention those things now, Mr. Chairman, it is because I have gained the impression that if we continue being prophets of gloom and doom in this way, and to sow doubt and anxiety in the minds of people, we shall create, here in Canada, a class of revolutionaries, which will

grow in strength, in power and in number at times of economic recession like the one we have known the last two years, when there was unfortunately too much unemployment. It is in the minds filled with doubt and anxiety and it is in homes where people suffer that communism can be sown to develop and eventually spill over and lead to devastation.
I can understand that politicians would want to say that everything is wrong and try to gain some political advantage among a certain class of people by exploiting a certain uneasiness which may exist within the nation. But such an attitude, in my opinion, is not that of a good Canadian, because a policy like this one when stretched too far, when exaggerated as it has been by members of the opposition, is likely to give rise to concern and even terror in the minds of the people, and could easily lead a country, where everything is good, great and prosperous, where freedom prevails like nowhere else, to the tragic situations in which other countries exposed to revolutionary movements find themselves and to the crises which accompany communism wherever it is successful.
Mr. Chairman, I listened with great interest earlier to the remarks of the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) and I told him too that is is always with a renewed pleasure that we listen to him in this house. He suggested that the program of the Liberal party should be implemented, because, according to him, it woult result in a prosperity unknown to us up to now. I wonder, Mr. Chairman, why the Liberals did not think about some of those points during the 22 years they sat on the treasury benches.
There was no unemployment in those days; we had prosperity.

Mr. Chairman, a report on the economic prospects, prepared by Canada's outstanding economists, forecast, in 1956 and 1957, the economic difficulties we experienced in 1958 and 1959; however, our friends of the opposition, knowing quite well that that report would certainly not help them on the hustings, chose to hide it because the people would have realized by reading it, that it was not with those who had run the country during 22 years, that Canada would achieve prosperity but with the Conservative government which, after its election, succeeded in getting our economy out of the rut where it had been left by the Liberal party. If we are enjoying a certain degree of prosperity today, if today we have progress and if we can look to the
Supply-Labour
future with confidence, surely we do not owe it to any advice given us in this house or elsewhere by the hon. members of the opposition, but rather to the wisdom, skill and intelligence shown by the leaders of the Conserative party in introducing social and economic measures that have brought the country its present state of prosperity.

Mr. Bennett used to talk like that.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the associate minister would permit me to ask him one question?

If the hon. member will permit, I shall finish my remarks in about two or three minutes and then I will be delighted indeed to answer all his questions. Mr. Chairman, I say to this committee that in our opinion the Canadian people have every reason to be proud of the performance which has been demonstrated by the members of this government in the finding of solutions to the economic problems which faced this nation. The problems were great and it was indeed difficult to find the proper solutions.
The members of this government worked many hours in order to find what they considered to be the right formulas for the Canadian economy. They had the help of all those who in their opinion knew something about these economic problems. They requested the co-operation of all those Canadian citizens interested in the future of Canada and the welfare of its citizens. It is through this co-operation of the state, of capital and of labour that we have arrived at the present successful conclusions.
A moment ago the hon. member for Essex East was suggesting that in order to get more and more prosperity we should follow the program that was enunciated at the Liberal convention which took place here in Ottawa last January.
Hear, hear.

May I say this to the hon. member, that if he reviews the various points of this great program to which he refers, he will realize that most of the measures contained in it have already been put into effect by the present Conservative government.
Oh, oh.

If the hon. member looks still more closely and if he goes back to the authors who describe what socialism is, he will find out that the other measures he

Supply-Labour
suggests are purely socialist measures which possibly could be understood if they came from the mouths of the members of the new party but which cannot be comprehended when they come from members of this once great Liberal party, which at one time could describe itself as the party of free enterprise but which today is more or less a modified version of the so-called new party.
I am very much afraid that if the only formulas the hon. members of the opposition have to suggest are those which they expressed during that great convention of theirs which took place last January, the Canadian people will not find much comfort or much solace in these suggestions. I am confident, on the contrary, that the Canadian people today appreciate the fact that if there is prosperity in this country it is due to the enlightened leadership of the right hon. Prime Minister, the members of his cabinet and the members of the Progressive Conservative party of which I am a proud member.

Mr. Chairman, the associate minister was kind enough to say he would be glad to answer all the questions I might ask about his speech. However, I do not think I will take up the time of the committee by going into all the irrelevancies, foreign and domestic, in the speech to which we have just listened. I have a hard, practical question I should like to put to the minister.
He talked about the desolate economic state of this country as revealed in a secret report, which his friends were apparently too stupid to appreciate at the time until they found a report in a drawer. If the conditions were so bad, surely these bright people, these paragons, might have found that out for themselves.
Question.

I have as much right to speak in the committee as anyone else and I am, after all, speaking about the only thing in the speech of the minister that was relevant. What I am doing is laying the foundation for a very simple question. Could the minister explain this. If the economic condition of Canada was so dreadful and so menacing in 1957, and if we have now reached new heights of prosperity, as he has said we have, under the enlightened leadership of the present government, why was it that in 1957 some 280,000 people came to this country from abroad and found employment and a chance to make a living here and this year barely a quarter of that number are going to come, and practically none of them are coming to look for work because they know that is not worth doing?

I should also like to ask the hon. gentleman how it happens that if conditions were so dreadful in 1957 and are so wonderful today, there are more than twice as many Canadians looking for jobs today as there were in August of 1957?
Mr. Chairman, I have said, and I repeat, that in 1956 and 1957 those who studied the economics of the nation could see the dark clouds looming on the horizon, and they said so in a report.
That is not true, of course.

It was only because hon. members opposite knew that it would be dangerous, after 22 years of power, to tell the Canadian people all was not rosy on the Liberal horizon that they kept this report carefully hidden. The hon. member has mentioned that 280,000 people came to this country in 1956 or 1957.
It was 1957.
It is true that this year the number has decreased.
To less than a quarter.

This number has decreased because the hon. members of the opposition, whether it be in this house, on television or on radio, have said too often that there was no future in Canada, and that this was a land of despair. It is because of this that people from abroad are afraid to come here and have refused to come here.
However, I can assure the hon. member that in view of what is happening at the present time this situation is bound to change in future years, because at long last, thanks to the actions of this government, people abroad realize that Canada is a land in which it is pleasant to live and not the land of distress which has been described by hon. members of the opposition.
Because there are fewer Liberals.

Mr. Chairman, there is one other matter on a more personal level. I do not recall that I, or any of my colleagues, have ever called the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate names or accused him of stupidity. Frankly, may I say that I find the word "stupid" rather unparliamentary and surely it is out of place in the present debate. I do not hold it against the hon. member for using such words, but I believe his stature would grow in this house and elsewhere if he respected those who engaged in debate with him as much as we try to respect the hon. member when he rises to express his views in this house.

If the minister will permit me, Mr. Chairman, I think perhaps he misunderstood what I said. I suggested that the minister was himself accusing his colleagues of stupidity, not that I was. I would explain to him very briefly and very simply why I say that, and I think it is very important.
The minister has asserted, as his leader asserted on January 20, 1958, that in a secret document some economists predicted a recession and that this document was hidden. That document was written in January of 1957 apparently by gentlemen with greater prophetic gifts than the leaders of the Conservative party. That was the point I was making, that today the minister has said what the Prime Minister said in January of 1958, that some people working for the federal government knew what was going to happen a year later, but that the Conservative leaders did not know. Why didn't they know, if the signs were so clear? Is the minister saying, and was the Prime Minister saying, that they were, to use the word I used, so stupid that they could not see those signs although some economist in a back room could see them? If so, why have they chased those economists out of the public service and stopped issuing those reports? If these men were so valuable why did hon. gentlemen opposite not keep them instead of getting rid of them? The fact is that months after the present occupants of the treasury benches had taken office the government was still saying there was nothing serious about the employment situation. When the Prime Minister met the premiers in November of 1957-I have not got the document here, but I could get it- he told them: there is a very temporary situation, but we are going to correct it in a few short months. He told the premiers: do not worry, it is nothing serious at all. Remember that the Prime Minister had been in office from June to November, that is to say, for five months, and if he was not stupid it was certainly careless of him not to have discovered this information in the meantime and found out what it was that the economists knew that he himself was not bright enough to see for himself. And, indeed, no other Canadian was aware of it, because anyone who reads that document objectively will realize that it never said what the Prime Minister made it say by picking out bits and pieces and leaving out all the rest. What it did say was that the rate of growth was going down, and Mr. Harris said the same thing in almost exactly
Supply-Labour
the same words in his budget speech well before the election. There was no deception. There was nothing of that sort. The fact of the matter is that in the year 1957 practically every Canadian was employed all through that year though we received, in that same year, the greatest addition to our population from abroad that we have had since 1913-282,000 people. Practically all of those people found work and most of them are still here and looking after themselves.
On a point of order. I regret to interrupt the hon. member, but I should like to ask him this: is he asking a question or making a speech?

I am making a statement in response to the minister's request that I should not accuse him of being stupid. I started out by saying that I was not accusing him of stupidity but that he was accusing his colleagues of stupidity or, to say the least, of carelessness.
Then again, on December 10, 1957 the Minister of Labour himself went to Montreal -this quotation has been referred to year after year and if anyone challenges it I shall produce it. I do not think the minister will challenge it. Well, the Minister of Labour has said on that occasion that there was no recession, that there was no serious unemployment.
Seasonal.

Yes, seasonal, as my friend from Maisonneuve-Rosemont has just reminded us. He said it was just seasonal. Even in December, six months after this government came to office, they had not discovered this terrible situation that some economist in the back room somewhere knew all about the previous March. If that is not a confession of stupidity or a confession of carelessness or a confession of incompetence, I do not know what is. And that is really what the minister's statement amounted to.
The minister cannot get around this other fact that at any time in 1957 unemployment was a great deal less than it has been in any year since in a comparable month-a great deal less-and in the month of August, 1957, it was less than half of what it is today.
The plain fact of the matter is that when members of the government say: why did you not put into effect when you were in office these recommendations you have made regarding unemployment, the answer is that we did not do so for the good reason that at no time after the war was there any persistent unemployment which necessitated such

Supply-Labour
measures. There was, certainly, unemployment in two winters-quite serious unemployment-and at that period the St. Laurent government did not waste any time. They called the provinces together and my hon. friend from Essex East put before them a scheme for unemployment assistance which was accepted by the provinces and which, fortunately, was put into operation by a Liberal government. If it had not been there would have been a great deal more suffering than there has been in the last four years during a period when the Prime Minister promised there would be no suffering as a result of unemployment as long as he was prime minister.
The hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate has once again referred to the stupidity of members of the government-
Self confessed stupidity.
He says that at that time we lacked the brightness which, he believes, illuminates his own side of the house.
That is obvious.

The hon. gentleman referred at length to this report which was so carefully hidden away from the eyes of the Canadian public, and he has referred at length to the speech which was made in January of 1958 by the Prime Minister in this house. It seems to me that if he and his friends remember the effects of that speech it would be best for them in view of the eventual results to forget it. We on this side, of course, are far too courteous and polite ever to call an hon. member of this house stupid or lacking in brightness, but I am afraid that if the hon. member continues in this vein it will be the people of Canada who will call him stupid and lacking in brightness.

On a point of order. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate will, I am sure, allow me as a backbencher to correct his figures regarding unemployment. I should like to ask him the authority for his statement that there is more unemployment today than at any time in earlier years.
From the bureau of statistics. I happen to have the figures right here on my desk.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: That is hardly a point of order. The hon. member can carry on later. The hon. member for Fort William-

The Associate Minister of National Defence who has just finished a speech on this subject of unemployment is to be congratulated on his faith and belief in the

government of which he is a member. He believes the government is meeting the employment and economic problems of the country. However, we on this side cannot find evidence to substantiate the belief that a solution has been found to these problems.
I do not wish to be analytical or controversial in discussing the estimates of the department presided over by the genial Minister of Labour, for whom I have great respect as a friend of long standing and as the chief executive officer of a most important department of government, but I have one or two questions in which I am particularly interested because they affect my own constituency to no small extent.
The first is the fact well known to this house that the city of Fort William needs new quarters to accommodate the unemployment insurance office, which now occupies a 70 year old building with no sanitary facilities available to the hundreds of people who visit this office daily. I have pointed out to this house on several occasions the deficiency of office space in which this important department is housed. The Minister of Labour informed me two years ago that plans for a new building were being drawn up and that he hoped it would soon be built to accommodate the staff, now subject to the worst possible labour conditions imaginable.
I visited the offices in question on several occasions. The last time I was there was the last week in August of this year. The basement was flooded-it had rained during the night. The corridors were crowded. I could hardly distinguish the office workers from the job seekers. I doubt whether there is a national employment office anywhere in Canada with facilities as poor and inadequate as those at Fort William, which serves an area of 70,000 people.
The minister is well aware that the Department of Public Works owns a central site which was formerly occupied by an armoury now demolished. I should like to hear from him what happened to the plans for the new building, which incidentally when built could accommodate other federal department services now renting from private concerns.
The unemployment situation at the lake-head has eased somewhat, as was expected, and thanks to the defence production program announced by the Minister of Defence Production a few weeks ago industrial plants in the eastern part of Ontario are now busier than they were in the past and the employment outlook is brighter. Canadian plants are beginning to reap the reward from purchases of defence equipment such as aircraft and heavy equipment of all kinds, but unfortunately the plants which are getting the largest share of orders are concentrated in

the eastern parts of the country, chiefly in Toronto and Montreal. While the plant of Canadian Car and Foundry Co., Limited at Fort William is now engaged in the manufacture of prefabricated movable homes for the armed services in the Arctic regions, I am convinced that it should share a larger proportion in the defence production program for Canada. Instead of employing a few hundred people, it should employ a few thousand. I beg the minister to use his influence with his colleague, the Minister of Defence Production, to try and equalize the distribution of defence orders more equitably than has been the case in the past.
The announcement of the minister that the government will contribute to an expanded municipal winter works incentive program to go into effect on October 15 next was, by and large, well received. However, while it includes projects hitherto not allowable under previous legislation, it does not fully meet the requirements of assistance which would spur the municipalities into a program of public works that would absorb a far greater number of men from the ranks of the unemployed.
What the municipalities want is to have the government share in the cost of materials. If such a policy were adopted, it would provide employment for twice the number of men, to say nothing of providing an increase in employment in the manufacture and supply of materials and services as a result of the program.
During the past several years efforts have been made by municipalities, by individuals and by organizations to stimulate winter employment. As an example, the lakehead unemployment advisory board has carried on a "do it now" winter work campaign for some years, and with great success. This committee is composed of men and women dedicated to the welfare of the community who have spent hours at every meeting trying to find some means by which to alleviate the vicious problem of unemployment. I sat in at some of their meetings and I know the sincerity of purpose of these people representing a cross section of the population of the cities of Fort William and Port Arthur. Not the least among the members are the managers of the unemployment insurance offices of both cities, whose zeal and dedication are indeed worthy of praise. I congratulate the department for having men of such high calibre at the head of these offices.
Winter construction now is not what it used to be. With the advancement and adoption of new techniques, construction undertaken in the winter months is of a quality equal to that undertaken in other seasons and therefore there should be no hesitation
Supply-Labour
in stimulating construction in the winter. Contractors should assume greater responsibility in their bidding on projects for construction during the winter.
The co-operation of all levels of governments, and that of individuals, organizations, architects and contractors is required to obtain the maximum construction activity during the winter which alone can ensure a vast improvement in the winter employment situation.
The August issue of the Bank of Montreal's Business Review notes that while everyone agrees high levels of employment are desirable, there is disagreement as to ways and means of achieving this aim. The publication summarizes the findings of the special committee of the other place on manpower and employment, which findings have contributed to a better understanding of the unemployment problem. And here I should like to say that if the other place had done nothing else during the year, the submission of their report alone would fully justify the existence of the upper house.
The review goes on to say that the Senate committee believes that a slower rate of growth, coupled with changes in Canada's basic economic structure, are the principal factors accounting for high unemployment. There was a decline in the rate of capital investment, so that a large portion of the labour force was displaced from construction and capital industries, without the opportunity arising for absorption in other kinds of work. Finally the review quotes the committee's own summary in these words:
There is a changed world environment. There are new trends and new circumstances in our society at home. These require re-thinking and a willingness to re-examine our priorities, our methods, and our machinery of economic policy. Continued progress depends on the ability to adapt, to solve new problems, and to take advantage of new opportunities.
The committee responsible for the statement which I just read has certainly rendered a public service of inestimable value in contributing toward a better understanding of the unemployment problem.
One cannot speak on unemployment without thinking of the melting unemployment insurance fund. In tracing the history of the fund, we find that when it was established in 1940 it was designed to be stable and self perpetuating. The act, which provided for a contribution of 20 per cent by the government, 30 per cent by the employee and 30 per cent by the employer, stood at $900 million by March, 1957. By March, 1958, it had declined to $754 million. By March, 1959 to $512 million and by March, 1960 to $383 million. I am informed that as of August 30, 1961 it was at $140 million.

Supply-Labour
Unless something is done, and done soon, it will not be many months before the fund will have reached bottom. This happened notwithstanding the government's action of two years ago, which increased by 30 per cent the rates payable by employees and employers.
It is true that the number of weeks allowable for benefits under the act was extended from 36 to 52. Is the government considering another boost in the rates which employees and employers are now paying?
Drastic remedial measures are needed now. A blood transfusion of approximately $200 million is necessary to put the fund back at a level where our present unemployed may be assured subsistence payment until they can find gainful employment again. And I submit that the only source this money can come from is the federal treasury.
The one-time surplus unemployment fund of $900 million is no longer self-sustaining.
Apart from the causes of poor investments, this diminution has been brought about because of relatively high unemployment with which this government has been unable to cope.
I wish to have the permission of the committee to insert in Hansard a table having to do with the number of claimants for unemployment insurance. The source of this information is the Canadian Statistical Review of March, 1961. If the committee wishes I can read it.

As I have already mentioned, when the fund was set up unemployment insurance was established for the purpose of giving workers some protection against loss of income during brief periods of unemployment. Since then, the brief periods for which the fund was designed have developed into an all-year-round chronic jobless problem.
The fund is no longer looked upon to serve its original purpose as a stopgap for people between jobs, but rather as a welfare agency, the only source to which the unfortunate unemployed can turn.
[Mr. Badanai.1
I do not minimize the seriousness of the situation into which the government, unwittingly perhaps, has fallen, but it cannot be denied that a major reappraisal of the unemployment insurance system should be proceeded with without delay.
I am sorry to say this, but I must say it. This government's worst enemy, is its attitude of procrastination when confronted with major issues requiring major remedies.
One of the solutions may be that which was recommended by the Canadian welfare council before the manpower committee of

the Senate to the effect, that the national employment service should be separated from the unemployment insurance commission. This separation could lead to a number of important changes in the machinery for the handling of both employment and compensation for unemployment.
With regard to compensation for unemployment, there are reasons to believe that there are instances where a too rigid interpretation of the act affecting seasonal workers, especially those in the building industry, has worked considerable hardships on those people who, as a result of the strict interpretation of the act, were denied unemployment insurance benefits.
Moreover, a new interpretation of the act, which I think was never intended, is evident by the denial of unemployment insurance benefits to tradesmen, such as carpenters, plasterers and brick-layers, only because they accepted employment from individuals and notwithstanding the fact that stamps have been provided for their books. It seems to me that this new interpretation should be reexamined at the earliest possible moment.
On the other hand cases have been reported where some individuals have cashed in on a loophole in the unemployment insurance regulations. An example was reported a few months ago in an editorial of the Financial Post. I do not recall the exact date or month; it might have been in October or November, 1960. It concerns a family living in Winnipeg who had earned $10,205 in a year while drawing unemployment benefits. Here is how it was done, according to the report.
The husband earned $85 a week as a carpenter and was laid off in December, 1958, just as he bought a building lot and poured a concrete basement. His wife, a garment worker, stayed at her $30 a week job, while he signed for jobless pay, claiming a nine-year old son as a dependent. He got $36 a week in benefits. This also entitled him to earn $18 a week as an "allowable" income and he promptly got a job for one day a week that paid $16.50. He mortgaged the lot and built his own home with money he borrowed. He worked four days a week on his house and one day at his carpenter's job. Several months later, while still unemployed, he sold the house for a profit of $4,860. Then, he promptly went back to work full time.
To sum up this family income: salary, June to December, 1958 at $85 a week, $2,210; unemployment insurance benefits December, 1958 to July, 1959 at $36 a week, $1,080; allowed income $16.50 a day for the same period or $495; his wife's earnings, $30 a week or $1,560; profit on the sale of the house, $4,860; total income, $10,205 or $194 a week. In January, 1960 he was laid off again. He
Supply-Labour
got another one-day-a-week job, bought a second lot and, according to my understanding, has now completed another house and will probably repeat the performance of the previous year.
The reason for bringing this particular episode to the attention of the government is to show that our present regulations are inadequate to control a situation such as I have tried to describe. There is no regulation to stop anyone from duplicating the performance of this person whose name I do not know.
There is no law to prevent a man out of work from building a house, a boat or furniture, and I am not advocating that there should be. Indeed, I commend any person for his enterprise in trying to keep himself employed. But if it can be shown that the income of such self employed persons is above a ceiling and that therefore they should not be entitled to receive unemployment insurance benefits, there should be some means whereby the regulations can be so amended. In other words, there must be a better way of operating an insurance scheme.
Perhaps consideration should be given to setting up two separate systems with separate funds, one for seasonal workers and the other for non-seasonal workers. The latter fund would serve non-seasonal workers, which was the original purpose for which the unemployment fund was established, to give regular workers some degree of protection against loss of wages for brief periods of unemployment. Such a fund should be as nearly self sustaining as possible. The other fund would require substantial annual assistance from the government.
In any event, the government has to make a decision soon. It cannot postpone the day of decision indefinitely. The question of what is to happen to the fund and how it is to be supplemented before it has all melted away and only drops remain is of course the responsibility of those who sit on the treasury benches. We in the opposition can only hope and pray that conditions will improve to such an extent that fewer people will need the assistance of the unemployment insurance fund in the future.

Mr. Chairman, before this session resumed on September 7 I for one had made a pledge to myself that for the balance of the session I would use the greatest of self restraint because I am one of many Canadians who feel that this session which started last November has produced far too much talk and far too little action. However, I find it extremely difficult in a situation such as this to exercise that self restraint when, for example, we hear the Associate Minister of National Defence painting such a rosy picture of the present economic

Supply-Labour
situation in Canada and when we realize that to paint such a picture he had to make use of comparisons with the cannibals of South Africa and the poor downtrodden people of South America. Surely the time of the house should not be wasted with such comparisons. Since when are we going to say that our situation is so wonderful by comparing it with that of the thousands of illiterate, downtrodden people in South America? Why does he not make comparisons with the people of the British Isles, Europe, the Scandinavian countries, Australia and New Zealand if he wants to make proper and sensible comparisons with regard to economic conditions? Instead, as I say, he compared Canada with South America, Cuba and so on, not realizing that we are as guilty as anybody for the present situation in Cuba. When the Cuban people tried to lift themselves up by their bootstraps, what did we do? We chased them straight into the arms of the Russian bear, possibly irrevocably. I think the time of the associate minister could be put to better use in this house.
I also think that the Canadian people are not too impressed by the endless statistics we hear from the hon. member for Essex East. I think a great many Canadian people realize that for 94 years we have had the Liberal pot calling the Tory kettle black and they are becoming fed up with this situation.
The best years in Canada's history.
I think it is time that both the government and the official opposition realized that it is the system to which they both subscribe so slavishly which is the cause of the problems that we now have.
Nonsense.

I think they should realize, as the associate minister said, that things are changing. Surely one of the greatest indications that things are changing was given to the Canadian people in the month of August when there took place in this very city the largest political convention ever held in this country, which was attended by people who are fed up with the old system.
And when you could not agree on giving people jobs, when you disagreed with Eugene Forsey, when you said you would not guarantee people jobs.
How many farmers were there?
Never was there a party whose bankruptcy was so well displayed as by that disagreement.

Mr. Chairman, possibly I have underestimated the effect that the convention had on the hon. member, especially when just the very mention of it raises a storm such as we have just witnessed. As I say, my resolve was to restrain myself, and while I am greatly tempted to continue further along this line I will try to come back to my original intention to restrict my remarks as much as possible. I should like to deal at this time with just one matter which I raised in the house some time ago. I believe hon. members will recall that on April 25 last I had occasion to raise a grievance in the house with regard to certain alleged working and living conditions at Moosonee having to do with a contract being carried out by the Carter Construction Company.
I make no apology for the grievance I raised at that time. It was based on information which had been supplied to me by letter from a union representative and also through personal contact with men from my constituency who had worked at Moosonee and who reported on the conditions there when they returned to Timmins. However, on the day that the house recessed in July, I believe, I received a letter from the same Carter Construction Company which reads as follows:
On April 25th last you commented on the floor of the house concerning a report that found publicity in several daily newspapers of Ontario, that had been made by Mr. Harry Hegge, a business agent for the carpenters union, regarding the working and living conditions on a project that we have under contract for Defence Construction Limited at Moosonee, Ontario. You might be interested to know that a contract has been signed between our company and the carpenters union for a period of one year on this project, and in the course of the contract negotiations, we brought to the attention of Mr. Andy Cooper, the national vice-president of the carpenters union, and Mr. Brodack, secretary of the carpenters local 1669 in Port Arthur that we resented these malicious and false statements that had been made by their union organizer, Mr. Hegge. I felt that, as you had taken the trouble to comment on this situation at Moosonee, it is only proper that you should have a copy of the letter of apology for your files wherein the union regrets the statements made by Mr. Hegge and states that they were "proven by investigation to be false and malicious".
Before I put this letter on the record in regard to this matter, I should like to deal with what happened in the interim between the time I raised this grievance in the house and the time I received this letter. Many of you may recall that conditions went from bad to worse and finally ended in a strike in this particular project. I am not sure of

the exact duration of the strike, but it lasted for some weeks and was finally settled by the agreement to which Mr. T. N. Carter referred in his letter. Enclosed is this copy of a very brief letter, and I quote:
Dear Sirs:
During our discussion with you concerning the above labour dispute, it was brought to our attention that statements made by our representative on the Moosonee project, Mr. Harry Hegge, that appeared in the various newspapers in southern Ontario, primarily the March 14 issue of the Globe and Mail, and also were quoted in Hansard, are for the most part wrong and grossly exaggerated, and were proven by investigation to be false and malicious statements.
I have found that the construction camp that you operate at Moosonee is well conducted and orderly and that the food being served the men is normal construction camp food, and that your camp is kept in a clean condition.
It is to our regret that our representative, Mr. Harry Hegge made these statements that have been so embarrassing to you.
Well, Mr. Chairman, needless to say I was rather shocked when I received this information. I was shocked particularly in view of the seriousness of the original charges and in view of the reports that had been given to me by men who had worked on this project. I also wondered if these statements were as false as they are now represented to be, and if so why had the situation deteriorated into a strike which in due course was settled. I made some inquiries and I was told that because of the fuss that was raised, both by the report and by my raising the matter in this house, the Carter Construction Company had been taken off the list of preferred contractors for defence projects, and in order to regain their status there must be some reply to these serious charges. I am told also that the strike at the camp was for $2.50 per hour in wages and the settlement was $2.85 an hour. This is the first time, to my knowledge, that any bargaining unit has gone on strike for a certain figure and has settled for a figure in excess of their demands. As I say, I am told that this was one of the conditions in order that the Carter Construction Company regained its previous status. They settled for 35 cents an hour more than was being requested, and in return received this letter of abject apology.
Now, Mr. Chairman, this is a rather shattering experience for any hon. member who in good faith raises a grievance on the floor of this House of Commons, then finds he has been undercut in this fashion. I think it is to the discredit of any trade union, be it the carpenters and joiners union or any other, to pull off a deal like this. I think they should be roundly condemned for doing so. I think this is something that we can do
Supply-Labour
without in this country. Any trade union that will pull a thing like this, in my opinion, does not deserve much credit.

Mr. Chairman, much could be said about the efforts of the Minister of Labour and his department in connection with unemployment and other problems. In taking part in this debate, I should like to point out the improvement shown in the twin cities of Kitchener and Waterloo since the first of the year and also the great benefits derived from the location of vocational and technical training schools there. The number of unemployed in these two cities, as well as other parts of the county, has dropped at a steady rate since January 1, 1961. This statement was made by the manager of the unemployment insurance office in Kitchener, and he added that the downward trend in unemployment has not hit bottom yet but should continue for some time as the economic situation brightens.
Construction workers made up the big portion of the unemployed, along with labourers, carpenters, painters, electricians, plumbers, cement finishers and plasterers. Millions of dollars worth of construction projects have been started and many others pending, and these are bound to have an effect on the employment situation. Amongst the projects which have made fine progress are the B.F. Goodrich new plant, the new brewery, and the new addition to St. Mary's Catholic hospital which will make this one of the finest hospitals in Canada.
Recently the Department of Labour announced the approval of technical and vocational school additions for the Eastwood collegiate in Kitchener and the Waterloo collegiate in Waterloo. These additions will be financed, as we know, by the dominion and provincial governments, the federal government bearing 75 per cent of the cost. This announcement, I am sure, was particularly approved by many of the citizens of my district. No doubt when they are completed they will be of great value to those who neglected to complete their education or, through other circumstances, were unable to take advantage of further schooling. I believe that these additions will provide work for many of our citizens.
I understand that nearly 70 per cent of the unmarried young people between the ages of 14 and 19 who are registered as jobless and living at home, have at least one parent working. In thinking of these young people I am led to commend the Minister of Labour and his department upon the introduction of measures concerning vocational and technical training which facilities have been increased to the extent of 50 per cent in Canada. The

Supply-Labour
federal government is to pay 75 per cent of the provincial contribution to the cost of these schools up to 1963. These young people living at home have a wonderful opportunity to improve their education and qualify for better positions and the security so necessary under modern conditions.
I hope that all people were able to read the statement recently made by our beloved Governor General in which he said:
Young people who leave school prematurely are cutting themselves off from most of the opportunities available in our country. Now, as never before, Canada's progress and security depend on the educational level, technical knowledge and skill of her people. It seems inevitable that those who leave school before graduation will miss most of the opportunities available in our country. They will cut themselves off from the possibility of training in Industry. They may have to face a lifetime of insecurity.
Recently, I read an editorial in my local newspaper the Elmira Signet written by R.
S.	Reid of the Kindersley Clarion. I should like to quote a part of it:
It has been a tragedy in every age and it is a greater tragedy in ours that so many of our most promising young people voluntarily cripple themselves. Their enthusiasm for life, their urge to be independent and self-reliant, their appetite for adventure-the very qualities which fit them to earn a place among our most useful and successful citizens-lead them instead to throw away their greatest chance of fulfilling their destiny. Eager to become a part of the adult world, they leave school before they have acquired an education that would enable them to make use of their natural gifts. The tragedy is greater today because our modern technological world has so little use for the half-taught-and such a desperate need for men and women with a full, well rounded education. Figures recently released by the national employment service clearly show that a high school education is a must for any person who wants to be sure of holding a job in our modern society.
Most young people must be aware, by this time, that the adult world is concerned about those who are unemployed in the nation. What they may not know is that persons with a less than grade 9 education form the greater part of the total of the unemployed.
Automation does create more jobs than it eliminates, but the new jobs are skilled jobs. In far too many cases the persons displaced by automation are unable to step into the new job it creates because they lack the education needed as a basis for training in the new work.
Our Minister of Labour, in bringing about new technical and vocational schools across Canada, is doing a most important job for those unfortunate people who may not have had the opportunity or ambition to carry on their studies in their younger days.
As a young man coming back from world war I in a disabled condition, I fully realized that I had neglected one of the great assets of life-education. In order to prepare myself for the future I attended the vocational school offered by our government under the Department of Veterans Affairs, and later
[Mr. Weichel.l
on attended night school for some years. Taking advantage of these opportunities has meant a great deal to me. May I say that such opportunities to attend vocational and technical schools are now offered to our young people by the government. As previously mentioned, Canada's progress and security depend upon the educational level, technical knowledge and skill of her people.
Today we are blessed with wonderful schools, colleges, universities and teachers who are ready and willing to bring that knowledge so essential to every boy and girl in this great country of ours. We have these additional vocational and technical schools, and a great majority of these unemployed young people between the ages of 14 and 19 years, along with others anxious to improve their education, should be impressed with these added facilities. These facilities will give them an opportunity to obtain an adequate education where they will have the chance of working up to the required income.
In concluding my remarks, Mr. Chairman, may I suggest that parents should take a greater interest in our youth. Yes, I know we supply them with the necessities of life, but after all that is only the materialistic side of things. What about the personal relationship of our boys and girls? No doubt we will admit that the basic education of any good citizen starts in the home, and there is no substitute for this first step in the over-all process. Like all proud parents, we expect much of our youth, and we must do so if our young country is to fulfil its ambitions.
Mr. Chairman, may I again commend the Minister of Labour and his department for their untiring efforts and impress upon all parents and others-indeed, upon all of us- that we have a very important part to play in the progress of Canada. One of these important efforts could be the encouraging of our youth, and others who neglected or did not have the opportunity of continuing their education, to attend these vocational and technical schools in order that they may provide for themselves a brighter future.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

Mr. Chairman, I had a call from one of the high officials of the city of Welland who told me that work was getting much slacker there at the present time. He said the number of unemployed was increasing, and no doubt the number drawing unemployment insurance will increase also.
So far this year there have been 1,090 welfare recipients, and the welfare paid out by the city of Welland has amounted to approximately $228,000. I do not give these figures to embarrass the government but because I wish to bring to the attention of the government some of the needs of the city of Welland and that area.
Welland does not seem to come within the category of the depressed area for double depreciation, according to the definition laid down by the government. Even so, Welland has had a great deal of unemployment for the last three or four years. There is a plant in Welland at the present time, Atlas Steel, that has a great expansion program in prospect. Consideration is being given by this company to a location for this expansion.
I understand that some high personages from other provinces have been in Welland offering certain definite considerations to Atlas Steel to locate in their respective provinces. No doubt one of the considerations offered has been that the plant will be located in an area where double depreciation would be allowed. Also rumours are prevalent there among these officials that another area in Ontario that is declared at the present time to be a depressed area eligible for double depreciation has been making a bid for this particular expansion program.
At the present time Welland is not in that category. I am informed that if they could receive more favourable treatment under the depressed area program there would be some likelihood of this plant staying in Welland. The minister told me today that as of now this plant would not get the double depreciation in Welland, while it could in these so-called depressed areas where double depreciation would apply. To me this seems rather discriminatory and unfair.

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. I am sure the hon. member for Welland does not wish to leave a wrong impression with the committee. He stated that I advised him that this plant would not receive double depreciation in Welland. The 90205-6-544
Supply-Labour
position is that Welland has not applied as a municipality for that designation. I am sure that if Welland applied for designation in a very simple way, perhaps by telegram or by letter, we would waste no time in looking at the situation to see whether Welland would qualify under the formula which has been set up, as some 19 municipalities and areas have already qualified. I do not want the impression to be left with the committee that Welland could not qualify. Welland has not applied in order to ascertain whether they could qualify or not.

I am sorry, Mr. Chairman, if I left the wrong impression with the committee. I intended to come to this point later and say that the minister told me Welland had not applied. However, if a plant moved from one part of the country to another they would not be increasing the wealth of the country but would be removing the facilities for production from one part of the country to another. I know that the Department of Labour-the Minister of Labour-has been flexible in reaching decisions as to whether certain areas can be included in the category to be declared areas to which the double depreciation allowance will apply. We know, for example, that one area was declared to be qualified although it was not in existence at the beginning of the period covered by the formula. I refer to Elliot Lake. In other cases, too, the minister has shown a degree of flexibility. I spoke to the minister this morning and he said that if Welland were to send in an application it would be given every favourable consideration. I thank the minister for this. I have talked to the mayor of Welland, and he said he would apply immediately.
I would appeal to the minister to give Welland the same degree of favourable consideration as he has given to some other places. Welland has been seriously affected by unemployment problems and I should not like to see a company leave the area to build an extension in another location because of this double depreciation feature if that feature were in any way to be a deciding factor. Atlas Steel has been in Welland for a number of years. The people of the county of Welland have reason to be proud of the Atlas Steel Company and of Mr. De Young, the president, now president of the productivity council, his staff and the employees. We should all like to see them remain in Welland; we should all like to see the expansion program carried out at the site of the main plant. The people of Welland would not like to see them move to another location which might be more desirable from the point of view of taxation as a result of some action of the government.

Supply-Labour
In view of Welland's unemployment problem I again appeal to the minister and to the government not to let this happen.

I have assured a number of those who have made representations to me that I would raise this matter at this particular time. I do not intend to take more than a limited number of minutes. I want to begin by endorsing wholeheartedly the contention made this morning by the hon. member for Essex East when he said he felt sympathy for the Minister of Labour on his having to take all the blame for unemployment in our nation. I agree with the hon. gentleman's contention that the question of full employment ought to be the responsibility of the government as a whole. 1 say this even at a time when we have the Minister of Labour sitting across on the other side of the committee. I rather regret, also, that the minister of labour in the former Liberal government had to take upon his shoulders almost alone responsibility for the level of unemployment which then existed. As is apparent if we consider the organization of the Department of Labour and the specific responsibilities assigned to the Minister of Labour, he alone would be completely unable to do much about what is, in effect, a major national calamity-or at least it is to those who are unemployed.
In the past mention has been made by the government of the national productivity council and its work. The council has been referred to again today. I was interested to hear the reply which the minister gave to a question asked by the hon. member for Leeds this morning. Any organization set up by the government which has been given the heavy responsibility of recommending ways and means of causing our economy to expand to such an extent that unemployment is reduced to a reasonable level should, in my view, certainly have met more often than three times, and I hope the minister realizes that this is a matter of such great significance to the welfare of all the Canadian people. Three meetings over a period of many long months are far from sufficient. The council ought to be meeting morning, noon and night until it comes up with answers which will be acceptable to the government and to the people.
The particular complaint I have this afternoon is one in connection with which I feel the national productivity council could really assist the minister. I have here a complaint, a letter and a resolution passed by local union 1064 of the united steelworkers of America in Sydney, Nova Scotia. I am impressed by the reasonableness of the proposals made by this local union. They do not

contend that there must be no readjustment in this industry in the Atlantic provinces. They do not even claim that the complete abolition of unemployment in the Atlantic region of Canada is possible. However, they do complain that the Avro company, which rules over the destinies of so many tens of thousand of Canadians, should be able to act in such an arbitrary and highhanded manner as it acts on occasion. They point out that more than 1,100 employees have been laid off at Dosco's Sydney steel plant, with a most recent lay-off of 606, including men who had been in the employ of the company since 1942. A resolution which was passed unanimously at a membership meeting urges that immediate steps be instituted by federal, provincial and municipal government heads to summon Avro officials to a meeting for the definite purpose of making commitments for the future of our economy. It may be that lay-offs are inevitable and that in the national interest they might, here and there, be the one and only thing that can be done. What these people are complaining about is the uncertainty. They are aware that Avro has plants in many parts of Canada and overseas, and they are unable to obtain from officials of Avro any indication how long they can reasonably expect to continue to be employed. It is in this regard that I should like to appeal to the minister to get his productivity council busy so that if there is to be relocation of either industry or labour, or both, these things may be arranged in an orderly manner, thereby averting the needless and unwarranted personal hardship which is imposed by decisions of a board of directors meeting, perhaps, in London, New York, Hamilton, Ontario, or elsewhere and deciding that it is in their interest to cause six or seven hundred men to be laid off, and having the power to pay no heed to the immediate effects that such an arbitrary decision must have on the lives of the individuals and of the communities in respect to a continuation of steady employment.
Our corporations are growing smaller, more powerful and limited in number. I feel the time has come when no Canadian corporation should be permitted to treat any individuals or community in the manner in which these people have been treated by those who own this plant. I am not contending that Dosco ought not to be expanded. I do not know why it should not be. If conditions warranted, perhaps Quebec, Nova Scotia and British Columbia could have plants to turn out our basic steel. However, as long as conditions continue as they are I believe the national productivity council,

the minister and indeed the government as a whole have the responsibility to ensure that individuals will not be dealt with arbitrarily as industries move from one area to another. The government should take steps to prevent arbitrary treatment such as that to which the people of Cape Breton island have been subjected over a period of several years.

Mr. Chairman, as I represent a riding where the working class makes up the greater part of the voters, I think I should at this point of our discussion of these estimates of the Department of Labour express the views of my voters, and therefore my own, with regard to unemployment.
Mr. Chairman, the word unemployment is in every Canadian citizen's mouth today, whether he is affected by unemployment or sincerely and loyally trying to work out some solution to alleviate as much as possible that social blight.
The causes of unemployment are many. It may be attributed partly to immigration, to automation, to the lack of primary industry in this country, however wealthy, to the lack of technical training among our fellow citizens, more particularly the young people, to incomplete education, or to the increase of the number of women workers on the labour market.
The causes may also be attributed to seasonal lay-offs as well as to seasonal unemployment or to competition on the world markets. Whatever the cause, Mr. Chairman, I think that unemployment is a blight which should be looked after with the greatest haste and care in order to avoid that certain revolutionary groups with communist leanings rouse the workers against established order, as they did before during the depression years, 30 years ago.
The right to work is a sacred right; nobody would deny to any person the exercise of his right to work, because it is a fundamental right. I know all hon. members, whatever their political affiliations, acknowledge this basic right. Now, if the workers have the right to work, I say that governments should look after the working class by taking the necessary steps to ensure that every individual who wants a job gets one.
Unemployment, Mr. Chairman, has often given rise to political controversies in this house, on the hustings, on television, on the radio and elsewhere. However, while we
