should not, on this side of the house, raise political issues in this respect, we cannot let go unanswered some more or less sincere remarks which opposition members like to voice in connection with unemployment. We cannot but, in all sincerity, honesty and loyalty, point out in this house, and to the whole Canadian people, everything this government has done to alleviate the effects of unemployment.
Everyone knows, Mr. Chairman, that the Conservative government has done much, in the few years it has been in power, to remedy the unemployment situation.
May I mention some measures which have been taken for the benefit not only of those who will read the newspapers, but also of some opposition members who stubbornly refuse to see what the Conservative government, aware of its responsibilities to the Canadian people, has done since it took office as far as unemployment is concerned.
As soon as it took over, this government carried out a considerable amount of public works in all municipalities which asked for them.
Obviously it was a remedy. It was not a measure intended to abolish or completely eliminate unemployment, but it was a definite and concrete measure. That winter works program caused a Liberal minister of the present provincial government in Quebec to say that there had been a reduction of about
48.000	in the number of unemployed, due to the implementation of the program.
It can be seen, therefore, that this Conservative administration due to the interest it showed in trade and the incentive it gave our domestic and international trade, as well as to the loans it granted small industries or businessmen, was quite successful in creating employment and opening new markets.
We should not forget also the absolutely concrete, logical and intelligent action of this government when it offered the provinces to contribute as much as 75 per cent of the cost of implementing a vocational training program for all workers wishing to use the benefits under the act. In fact, I was informed that in the province of Quebec, more than
3.000	workers availed themselves of these provisions, to the application of which the federal government contributes up to 75 per cent of the costs.
Mr. Chairman, the population and opposition members should be told of the considerable sums this government has put into the C.M.H.C. fund, for housing construction and

Supply-Labour
urban redevelopment. That initiative has greatly contributed to alleviating or checking unemployment.
Mr. Chairman, since the beginning of this debate, we have not heard a single opposition member explain the unemployment problem.
I would be tempted to deal with employment, but I feel that to find a solution to the problem, we must first consider the different types of unemployment and their causes. Those who have dealt with this problem in a somewhat more personal way have defined four types of unemployment.
Frictional unemployment results from defective functioning within the labour market. Incidentally, this type of unemployment may exist even at times of full employment and it is due to fluctuations among the various industries.
There is a second type known as cyclic unemployment, which is caused by the cycle of business, according to whether it proceeds slowly or at an accelerated pace.
There is also a third type known as seasonal unemployment which apparently is the nightmare of all northern countries.
There is, too, a fourth type of unemployment-technical unemployment. It is brought about, of course, by the introduction of new techniques into the industrial world.
Now, Mr. Chairman, it so happens that the riding I represent in this house is particularly striken by the three last types of unemployment: cyclic, seasonal and technical unemployment.
The present government has dealt with the problem arising from the fourth type, technical unemployment, and has suggested to the provinces ways and means of meeting this type of unemployment.
There is still seasonal unemployment, a situation that is to be found in all northern countries. We could obviously take more steps to lessen the effects of this category of unemployment; but, after all, it is due to nature.
Therefore, I believe there is an unemployment situation that should be called "general unemployment". It is due to a lack of cohesion in the distribution of the labour force. It is on this situation that I request the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) to get as soon as possible the necessary datas for economic planning, which involves a knowledge of labour demand in every industrial category, and the distribution of that demand according to the needs and the various categories of employees.

Mr. Chairman, unemployment is not only- those words are not mine-a federal responsibility. Whatever its causes or reasons, unemployment is not only a federal responsibility; it is also the responsibility of the provincial and local administrations, and even that of the unions. The heads of each of those administrative levels should assume their responsibilities in order to restore full employment in this country.
We read every day in the papers reports of some labour disputes that are more or less fair or reasonable, but I fail to understand that in times of serious unemployment, labour and management cannot agree in order to prevent as many strikes as possible. Considering the frightening number of millions of working hours lost through those strikes, it is of the utmost importance to urge labour unions, union leaders, labour and management also to assume their responsibilities in this field.
Mr. Chairman, as I said earlier unemployment is not only a federal responsibility, but also a provincial one, and I am not the one who said so. In this respect, I should like to quote the statement made by the ephemeral leader, Hon. Jean Lesage, head of the Liberal party in Quebec.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Chairman, judging by the applause, I think that the word ephemeral won the approval of the house; but it must be kept in mind that it means short-lived and that the Liberal leader will not last very long.
As I was just saying, the Liberal leader stated that unemployment is a provincial responsibility. Therefore, if we examine the current statistical data in the province of Quebec, and more especially those relating to unemployment in general, we find that it has declined everywhere in Canada, except in the province of Quebec, where it has increased in the last six months.
Therefore, we would ask the provincial government which declared that unemployment is a provincial responsibility to carry out its election promises and to set up a program to reduce the unemployment which prevails in the province of Quebec at the present time.
Every week, electors come to my office by the hundreds to tell me that Mr. Lesage, the premier of Quebec, has promised and even sworn that he would solve the problem of unemployment in the province. Yet, they

say, he is the first one to fire us from the jobs we hold with the provincial government.
If that is how some premiers intend to assume their responsibilities concerning unemployment, I call on the people to sweep the Liberals out of office, as they did in Ottawa, and we will take their place and strive to take efficient steps to fight unemployment.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few suggestions to relieve somewhat the unemployment which the Quebec provincial branch of the Liberal party ignores, and even to put an end to it in my province and in the constituency I represent.
I wonder if the Minister of Labour could not, in co-operation with the city of Montreal, undertake a huge project such as the construction of a scenic route all around the island of Montreal. As everybody knows, Canada's metropolis offers great advantages from the points of view of aesthetics, culture and education. In my opinion, we have somewhat neglected, until now, to develop Montreal's natural advantages. Consequently, I would ask the minister to discuss this matter with his colleagues so as to come to an agreement concerning a winter works project such as the construction of a scenic route around the city of Montreal, to reduce unemployment.
Moreover, as another way of creating jobs for the unemployed in the Montreal area, I wonder if the Minister of Labour could not, once more, co-operate with his colleague the Minister of Public Works and have a tunnel built under the St. Lawrence, in order to improve communications between Montreal and the south shore.
Also, Mr. Chairman, in order again to create jobs and reduce unemployment, which has become a serious problem in the province of Quebec since the Liberals have taken over, I would suggest to the minister to speed up large scale town redevelopment, so far as housing in Montreal is concerned.
Mr. Chairman, some time ago responsible persons made a study of the unemployment problem. I did not say that the former government should be blamed for it, nor should we now be. I did not say either that the provincial Liberal party was responsible, although some members of the opposition may be oversensitive on that issue since their election campaign is being turned against them.
With your permission, Mr. Chairman, 1 should like to quote a paragraph on future prospects in Canada:

There is evidence that the recession in the regular business cycle is coming to an end and that an economic recovery is appearing. The recovery factors have been operating for several months in the United States and, if they go on, they will spur a business readjustment in Canada in the months ahead. It is to be expected that such an improvement will contribute to increase employment and, as a result, reduce unemployment. Mr. Chairman, that is precisely what this Conservative government has done in the way of unemployment prevention, something the Liberals have always tried to prevent us from doing. Because we increased the housing money supply, members of the opposition called out that we were overloading the government's budget. When we wanted to make ready money available to industry and business, again, members of the opposition protested that we chose to uphold Mr. Coyne's destructive policies instead of promoting a normal and realistic economic expansion which would procure employment in this country.
But this is not from me, Mr. Chairman. If our good friends, who are a little ill at ease because of these arguments, would read the report of the Senate special committee on manpower and employment that was published on June 14, 1961, where the Liberal senators had majority, they will find that this Senate committee with a Liberal majority has just approved the very methods used by this government to fight unemployment.
Well, Mr. Chairman, if our friends want to be sincere and honest, they will admit that this government has done more than any previous government to fight unemployment. If they are not satisfied with that, let them ask their leader, Premier Lesage of Quebec, to do more than we have, because he has done nothing up to now.
Before I conclude my remarks, Mr. Chairman, I should like to correct certain statements made here this afternoon, especially by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill), to the effect that we never had so many unemployed as today, if I understood him correctly.
Well, Mr. Chairman, I have here the Montreal Star of September 19, 1961, where we read that in August, 1960, the number of unemployed, in thousands, was 352, and in August 1961, 323. This is a decrease of 29,000.
I wonder where the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate could possibly have

Supply-Labour
picked up his statistics. As the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) would probably put it, most likely from Martin's bureau of statistics; but I prefer to rely on those of the dominion bureau of statistics.
Mr. Chairman, I certainly would have more remarks to make, more particularly in regard to female workers on the labour market. From 1949 to 1959, the labour market has shown a 43 per cent increase in the number of female workers. Of course, always according to those statistics, it is said that most female workers are married. Well, that is a problem which we shall have to consider carefully, but, in my opinion, female workers contribute to the increase in unemployment among married men.
Therefore, I would ask the minister to take into consideration those few remarks I have just made, and at the same time I would ask our Liberal friends to be a little more serious and less politically-minded when they talk about unemployment.

Mr. Chairman, I felt I should wait until the hon. member for St. Mary had concluded before pointing out to him that I think he misunderstood what I said. What I said was that month for month in no year since 1957 has unemployment been as low as it was in 1957. I have all the figures right here in my hand. They are not from newspapers or anything else, but from the bureau of statistics. I will give the bureau of statistics figures for the month of August in the years from 1957 on. This is the labour force survey of persons without jobs and seeking work. In August, 1957 the number was 174,000; in August, 1958, 281,000; in August, 1959, 239,000; in August, 1960, 322,000, and in August of 1961, according to the latest release, 301,000.
How many were working?

That is not the point that was being discussed. I am merely correcting a point that the hon. member raised but since the question has been asked I will answer it. The proportion of the total population employed-
How many were working?

Perhaps the hon. member would just listen to the answer to his question. The percentage of the total population employed was higher in every month in 1957 than it has been in the corresponding months in any year since.

Mr. Chairman, I have to correct an experienced member of the house, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. He said that in 1957 the number of people employed was higher than ever before. Am I correct?

No, I did not say any such thing. What I said was that the number of persons unemployed was lower in each month of 1957 than it has been in the corresponding month in any year since. I gave the figures for the month of August and I am quite prepared to give them for any other month if the committee wants them. These are dominion bureau of statistics figures. I also made the assertion that the percentage of the total population which was employed was higher in each month of 1957 than it has been in the corresponding months of any year since.

If the corresponding numbers in each month were better, then I suppose the corresponding average for the year would be better than in any year before; otherwise the premise of the member would be false and would lead to a fallacy, which I do not doubt it is. I have here the report of the Senate committee on manpower and I should like to refer the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate to it. There have never been so many people employed in Canada as there are today. In 1950 there were 5,163,000 people employed, while in 1960 there were 6,403,000.
If I follow the argument of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, then the average is much lower in 1956 than in 1957. If I have the correct figures here, then it is also less in 1951, 1952 and 1953, perhaps because of the Korean war. I think the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate should refer to this report of the Senate committee on manpower.

I cannot allow those figures to go unchallenged. We know, of course, that practically every year there have been more people employed than the year before because we have a lot more people. What I was talking about was the percentage, and I think my statement will stand.

The latest figures released by the Department of Labour, in conjunction with the dominion bureau of statistics, show a slight improvement in the unemployment situation. The report for the week ended August 19 indicates that unemployment declined by an estimated 31,000. This stands out in sharp contrast to the figures for the Atlantic region where unemployment in-

creased by about 12,000. It seems, therefore, that despite all the encouragement we may get from the over-all picture as contained in this report to which I have just referred, it nevertheless appears that unemployment is still our most pressing domestic problem and is likely to continue so for some time to come.
I must confess that I was greatly impressed by the sharp contrast in viewpoint concerning unemployment between the hon. member for St. Mary and the Associate Minister of National Defence. The hon. member for St. Mary, who represents a workers' riding, still maintains, as we do, that unemployment is a very serious problem. No matter from what angle we may look at it, unemployment is a tragedy. It is a tragedy of human suffering. It is a tragedy of economic waste, of potential wealth, and a tragic waste of human skills and talents. This tragedy is heightened all the more when we see so many of the needs we have here in Canada and in the world which are still waiting to be filled.
Now, everybody seems to have some plan for solving this tremendous problem. The government called us together last November and announced a program for a massive assault on the unemployment problem. To facilitate that program, we of the opposition elected to forgo the time traditionally allocated to the speech from the throne. The minister, in the presentation of his estimates last March, referred to some of these measures and today the hon. member for Essex East put on the record a number of other proposals for our party. There are some who maintain that it is up to the government to solve this problem, that the government has the sole responsibility for finding jobs for people.
Personally, I cannot subscribe to this philosophy because it is not compatible with individual freedom. We have many lessons from history which indicate that when people are prepared to forgo or to sacrifice that responsibility and trade their freedom for security or for work, then the result has always been tyranny. I think it is reasonable to expect that if we adopt this kind of thinking, history is bound to repeat itself.

speechtext: The enlightenment about Saturday will depend on the enlightenment the house offers to me tomorrow about the progress of business. We will settle that tomorrow. Thursday, we will continue with the estimates of the Department of Labour, followed by the Department of National Health and Welfare. Then on Friday, in response to a number of requests, the following arrangement has been agreed upon: We will interrupt the study of the estimates on Friday to deal with the resolution concerning fitness and amateur sports on the understanding that Monday and Tuesday, which normally are for legislation, may be used for estimates if we so desire, on the same basis as last week, moving into supply without a debate or amendment. This has already been agreed through the normal channels, and if it is satisfactory Friday's business will commence with the resolution stage of the bill pertaining to fitness and amateur sport. If it is finished in good time on Friday we will revert to the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare. That carries us into Thursday and Friday, and tomorrow we will make a decision with regard to Saturday. If things move very quickly the third department to be considered will be national revenue.
I take it that the other two departments mentioned by the Minister of National Health and Welfare last night will follow if there is an opportunity.
